detail.abstract: Does a technology-oriented trade shock affect hiring scale or also occupational composition? We study Chinese firms during the 2018 U.S.-China trade war using approximately 900 million online vacancies, industry-level Section 301 tariff exposure, and AI Occupational Exposure (AIOE) index. Using tariff variation over time, we compare hiring across occupations within firms. Greater tariff exposure is associated with fewer vacancies and larger declines in higher-AIOE occupations. A one-standard-deviation increase in tariff exposure corresponds to an additional 0.9 percent decline in vacancies for occupations one standard deviation higher in AIOE. The negative gradient is concentrated in industries facing greater technology catch-up pressure and tighter competition. It is more pronounced among routine, non-cognitive, and non-STEM occupations, but attenuated for vacancies with higher qualification and task requirements. Posted wages and resume-based employment shares show similar patterns. These findings identify withinfirm occupational reallocation as an important margin of labor-demand adjustment following a technologyoriented trade shock.

title: Build, wait or strand? Estimated margin feedback and the transition risk of India's refinery expansion

detail.title: Build, wait or strand? Estimated margin feedback and the transition risk of India's refinery expansion

detail.abstract: India accounts for a large share of the world's planned refining additions just as global fuel demand approaches its peak. We value India's existing refineries and its expansion options under transition risk, replacing the usual assumed link between demand loss and refining margins with an estimated one. Using a 2000-2024 panel of the three benchmark refining centres, we estimate that a 1% fall in refinery utilisation lowers the benchmark margin by about 8.7% (2SLS; the weak-instrument-robust interval is wide, and we carry 6.6-12.9), while net capacity adjusts by only 11% of a utilisation gap a year. Refinery-level data for India show that margins depend on ownership, not complexity: private and joint-venture refineries earn about US$6.4/bbl more than state-owned ones. Propagating 5,000 probabilistic demand paths through this margin model, the transition removes a median INR 6.5 lakh crore (about US$75 billion, 41%) of the existing fleet's value, falling disproportionately on thin-margin state-owned plants. It raises the break-even gross refining margin of a 60 MMTPA greenfield refinery from US$10.0 to US$13.5/bbl. On the preferred estimates a private-type operator would build such a plant at once without the transition but not with it, although weaker margin channels reverse that verdict; a state-owned operator would not build on commercial grounds in either case at refining-attributable capital cost. Splitting the project into modules does not pay at standard scale economies. A reduced-form margin channel of the kind common in the literature understates the fleet loss by more than half.

title: Feasibility Conditions for Nuclear Fusion Electricity: The Ledger a Power Plant Must Meet

detail.title: Feasibility Conditions for Nuclear Fusion Electricity: The Ledger a Power Plant Must Meet

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no conflicts of interest.

detail.abstract: The record target gain of fusion ignition at the National Ignition Facility, fusion yield over laser energy on target, is 4.13, set on 7 April 2025. Yet target gain alone does not decide whether a power plant is feasible. This paper defines a wall-plug-to-grid ledger of four ratios: A, fusion energy per unit of grid electricity drawn by the driver; B, gross electricity per unit of fusion energy; C, the fraction of gross electricity left after auxiliary loads; and D = A × B × C, the electricity returned per unit spent. Net export requires D > 1; D ≥ 4 is adopted as the commercial benchmark. Using the published grid consumption of about 300 MJ per shot, the record shot gives A ≈ 2.87% and, with a thermal plant attached, D = 0.87% to 1.35%. Inverting the ledger gives the thresholds A ≥ 2.1 to 3.3 for D = 1 and A ≥ 8.5 to 13.2 for D = 4, shortfalls of 74 to 115 and 300 to 460. Per gigawatt exported it requires about 17 shots per second and, at illustrative prices, targets costing 0.10 to 0.24 US dollars each. For deuterium–tritium fuel a perfect direct converter raises B by at most 1.21 to 1.34, and the best converter efficiency yet measured raises it by under 4%. Raising B × C from 0.381 to 0.638 lowers the required A by a factor of 1.7, leaving a factor of about 220 to driver efficiency and target gain.

detail.abstract: Should a platform show all consumers all products, or at least those they like most? Or could it raise consumer surplus by mismatching some consumers: showing them only less-preferred products or even excluding them from trade? I show that in both monopoly and duopoly, mismatching can raise aggregate consumer surplus by inducing lower prices. In duopoly, consumer-optimal matching uses a cutoff policy: along each diagonal of equal valuation differences, consumers with lower valuations are matched only to less-preferred products, and some may subsequently be excluded. With independent uniform valuations, this raises aggregate consumer surplus by about 41% over full matching.

detail.abstract: Firms can comply with environmental regulation by changing production processes or by abating pollution after it is generated; yet the production margin remains largely a black box. This paper opens it using stage-level production, environmental, and financial data for Chinese steel firms. We exploit within-province variation in regulatory pressure under the 2016-2020 Good-Air Days targets in a difference-in-differences design. Firms facing greater pressure rely less on the pollution-intensive upstream stages and invest more in abatement. A one-standard-deviation increase in target intensity reduces pig iron input per ton of crude steel by 2.4% of its mean, implying a 2.2-percentage-point rise in scrap's share of metal inputs. Environmental investment rises by 49% of its mean, concentrated in air-pollution control. Pre-tax profit per ton does not fall. The production adjustment implies only a small reduction in reported SO2 emissions. Evaluations based solely on emissions or financial outcomes would overlook the production margin.

title: Contractual freedom versus tenancy law

detail.title: Contractual freedom versus tenancy law

declarations.declarationOfInterest: none

detail.abstract: We study a two-period principal-agent model of rental housing in which a landlord (principal) offers a contract to a tenant (agent). After the first period, a cost shock may occur that increases the landlord's cost of providing the apartment in the second period. Two scenarios are compared. In one scenario, there is full contractual freedom, while in the other scenario, there is a tenancy law requiring the landlord to continue renting in the second period if the apartment was rented in the first period. Under symmetric information, gains from trade in the tenancy law regime can never exceed those under contractual freedom. However, we show that when the tenant has private information, the tenancy law can lead to strictly higher gains from trade.

detail.abstract: This article critically examines the European Data Protection Board's initiative on the social acceptability of camera-enabled smart glasses, analysing the commissioned qualitative research alongside the Board's October 2026 statement and the Hamburg DPA's technical and legal assessment. It evaluates the relationship between the social evidence and the legal conclusions advanced, then reconstructs documented operating modes and data flows from the available technical evidence. Tracing processing across the device and connected services grounds a doctrinal analysis of user responsibility and controllership under the GDPR, situated within the wider law governing image capture and disclosure. The analysis distinguishes the wearer's personal photography from the provider's independently determined service processing and any separately established further use. It concludes that an ordinary request for visual assistance does not itself establish joint controllership; the provider's commercial purpose likewise does not automatically remove the household exemption from the wearer's private activity. Separating capture from publication also clarifies the interference requiring justification and the actor responsible. Effective safeguards retain legal significance without achieving absolute anonymity, while legitimate interests can support defined processing that satisfies necessity and the balancing test. These findings produce a materially different legal picture from the broader regulatory concerns and restrictive implications of the EDPB and Hamburg materials. Social acceptability can inform the assessment, but cannot replace attributing responsibility or create an independent condition of lawfulness. The article argues for supervision grounded in identifiable processing and applicable duties, with practical guidance explaining how lawful uses can proceed.

detail.abstract: Does competition between market makers over algorithm choice lead to the adoption of algorithms that produce competitive prices? We study strategic delegation of market making to learning algorithms. Market makers commit to Basic Q-learning or Clever counterfactual Q-learning and evaluate expected average monetary profit over the learning path. Clever can produce competitive prices when mutually adopted, but requires additional market data. In the baseline Basic-Clever game, mutual Basic is an equilibrium for every nonnegative data cost, whereas mutual Clever requires sufficiently cheap data. Strong adverse selection can also make Basic strictly dominant. Competition over algorithm adoption therefore does not guarantee competitive prices. Allowing delegation to misaligned Biased algorithms with distorted learning rewards can further worsen market quality.

detail.abstract: We study when the pursuit of an aspiration makes an actuarially fair risk worth taking. We analyze a static model in which an agent with aspiration-based preferences either faces a fixed fair risky option or designs any fair gamble over future income. Crossing the aspiration yields an extra reward and creates the only nonconcavity in the continuation payoff. We show that aspiration-driven fair risk arises when safe income lies in a unique gambling segment pinned by the aspiration. A common-tangent condition determines the failure and success targets of the optimal gamble. These targets depend on the aspiration and its reward, while income affects only the probability of success. Under logarithmic utility, the targets have closed form. Because the segment straddles the aspiration, even agents who have already attained it may prefer a fair gamble. The trigger is segment membership, not frustration. When aspirations are socially formed, aspiration-driven risk is non-monotone in inequality and strongest at intermediate inequality. The mechanism suggests that inequality can shape risktaking not only through resources, but also through the aspirations by which individuals evaluate risk.

detail.abstract: We estimate a profitability measurement model without return data and use it to select ten accounting ratios from thirty candidates. Across fifteen annual U.S. cross-sections, cleaner measures of latent profitability predict realized returns more strongly. Two aspects of measurement quality behave differently. The magnitude of the profitability loading largely reflects similarity to return on assets. By contrast, construct specificity-how clearly profitability dominates competing dimensions-distinguishes the better return predictors even after controlling for accounting construction and similarity to return on assets. The same ten ratios remain specific to the profitability dimension across all fifteen primary cross-sections. In implementation, measurement information is useful both for selecting ratios and for weighting a broader candidate set. A selector based on realized returns recovers about eight of the same ten ratios.

detail.abstract:
Software agents built on large language models and reinforcement learning are beginning to read filings, place trades, make payments and negotiate with one another on behalf of people and institutions. Agentic AI in Finance is a practical and analytical guide to this shift. It covers how financial agents are built, how they learn and what happens to markets when many participants are machines.

Part I builds a working trading agent in an afternoon, then systematically repairs its flaws. The repairs cover:

  • tools and memory
  • point-in-time data that prevents look-ahead leakage
  • honest evaluation, including off-policy methods and significance testing
  • deterministic guardrails against risk and prompt injection

Part II makes the agent learn. It covers reinforcement learning for allocation, hedging, market making and optimal execution, and the RLHF-to-agentic-RL methods now used to train tool-using language models. A multi-agent market simulator shows how shared models produce correlated decisions, herding, liquidity withdrawal and flash-crash dynamics.

Part III turns to markets in which agents deal with agents:

  • agentic commerce and payment protocols
  • identity, delegated authority and liability
  • auctions, pricing and negotiation, including evidence that learning agents can collude tacitly
  • market designs, such as batch auctions and agent-aware circuit breakers, that blunt speed races and coordination
  • supervision, concentration risk and a research agenda for regulators

Throughout, the book draws lessons from the rise of high-frequency trading and emphasizes five principles:

  • deterministic controls around stochastic agents
  • evaluation designed to disprove
  • diversity as a defense against systemic risk
  • transparency through agent logs
  • market design as part of the solution

detail.abstract: The ratio of U.S. Treasury bond and note principal to equity market value predicts stock market excess returns at horizons from one month to five years. At one year, it delivers in-sample and out-of-sample R 2 of 15.8% and 16.7%, well above those of established predictors, and certaintyequivalent gains exceeding 400 basis points annually for a mean-variance investor. The ratio also forecasts nominal dividend growth and corporate bond excess returns, and favorable cash-flow news and declining discount rates account for its return predictability about equally. High values coincide with low business investment, slow bank balance-sheet growth, and elevated fiscal policy uncertainty.

detail.abstract: Despite intensive securitisation of black earth and soil quality as existential for food sovereignty and human health, Europe has built no area-wide regenerative capacity by 2026. Soils remain predominantly degraded, nutrient density is declining, and dependence on dietary supplements is growing. This paradox raises the question why European securitisation remains largely performative, while China achieves measurable material progress in prioritised regions and the USA advances scalable practices through market-and incentive-driven approaches. The article shows that persistent biophysical inertia, high operational conversion risks, and governance that relies on non-binding targets and the promotion of individual management practices rather than measurable soil improvements generate a structural performance-outcome discrepancy. Institutional activity substitutes for material capacity building. The result is an ontological shift from threat management to performative self-stabilisation. Drawing on comparative processtracing, the study develops an outcome-oriented extension of Securitisation Theory.

detail.abstract: Performance Management Systems (PMS) have become a critical framework for aligning individual employee performance with overarching organizational objectives. Beyond evaluating past performance, PMS fosters continuous improvement, engagement, and development, enhancing productivity and motivation. The integration of sustainability goals within PMS creates a holistic approach to addressing global challenges, including climate change, inequality, and biodiversity loss. By leveraging structured goal-setting, feedback, and assessment processes, organizations achieve greater transparency, cost efficiency, and competitive advantage. This review examines the impact of sustainability performance management on organizational growth, highlighting its role in balancing financial objectives with ecological and social responsibilities. The findings underscore that sustainable performance management not only drives operational efficiency but also establishes a robust framework for achieving long-term success in a competitive global market.

detail.abstract: The OECD global minimum tax (Pillar Two) is built around a single GloBE Information Return, yet each implementing jurisdiction adds its own registrations, notifications, returns, portals and deadlines. These obligations are published piecemeal, often in the local language, across tax authority websites, and no public dataset records them in comparable form. This paper describes one that does. As at 4 November 2026 it records 77 Pillar Two filing obligations in the 22 of 25 tracked jurisdictions that impose them, each read from a tax authority or other government page. Deadlines are encoded as machine-readable rules, alongside the access step that must precede filing, penalties where an official text states them, and a dated log of 80 changes. Four patterns stand out. Central filing of the information return rarely ends local work: 16 of the 22 jurisdictions require a separate step that names the filing entity or confirms that the return is filed abroad. Although 46 obligations follow the OECD's 18-then-15-month clock, the earliest deadlines a group meets are local registrations and notifications, some due within 30 days. Only one authority states how long access to its filing channel takes to obtain. And in 12 of the 22, penalty amounts could not be confirmed from a primary text. The dataset is open for non-commercial use, archived with a DOI and maintained against the authorities' own pages.

detail.abstract: Problem definition: A city must spend a fixed seasonal budget against a mosquito-borne epidemic across wards and weeks. Allocation models in operations research usually assume treated areas stay treated and surveys stay true. In dengue neither holds: fogging fades within weeks and the epidemic grows weekly. We ask when to concentrate spending, when to start, and whether surveys pay. Methodology/results: We calibrate a ward-level vector-host model of Dhaka North and sweep adulticide efficacy, the share of adult mosquitoes a fogging round kills in the field, across ten instances. Two thresholds separate three regimes. At weak efficacy, full coverage from week one is worse than spreading the same money over the season: it delays the outbreak instead of suppressing it. At moderate efficacy, concentrating pays, but a later start beats an immediate one. At high efficacy, concentrating at once is best. No robustness check reverses the thresholds' order. Over the range spanning both, targeting guided by whole-ward case surveys trails uniform spraying at base costs, since surveys divert money from spraying; targeting pays if surveys cost a quarter as much. Where wards differ strongly in breeding capacity, larviciding known hotspots pays at moderate efficacy, and a reinforcement-learning agent learns this. In a weekly vector map where habitat control lowers carrying capacity, we prove no schedule of it stabilises vector extinction, while sustained adult killing eliminates vectors at high enough efficacy and coverage. Managerial implications: The best lever depends on field efficacy, which bioassays do not measure. At the reference efficacy, the first week of delay roughly doubles the peak, and a six-week full-coverage campaign matches the peak of season-long coverage within 1% at under a third the cost. For efficacy from 0.45 to 0.65, starting a concentrated campaign in week two minimises worst regret and expected peak.

detail.abstract:
Voluntary carbon markets are a market-based mechanism for the private sector to fulfil their net-zero emission commitments. They exhibit unique characteristics relative to traditional commodity markets, challenging price transparency and their ability to scale.

This paper develops a framework for estimating the market price of environmental integrity for carbon credits. Utilising a meta dataset of 15,000 AlliedOffsets prices and Sylvera credit ratings for 72 Agriculture, Forestry and Other Land Use projects, we assess the attributes influencing prices of carbon credits deliverable into the CME CBL N-GEO Futures market between 2022 and 2025. 

The framework offers a complement to futures-based price discovery, providing insights into the pricing of environmental integrity within voluntary carbon markets.

detail.abstract: Freud identified three wounds to human self-love: the cosmological, the biological and the psychological. A fourth, delivered by artificial intelligence, has been claimed by Mazlish (1993), Floridi (2014), Bratton (2024) and others, and Brunnhuber (2025) has already counted a fifth. This paper argues that the count is unstable because the wounds have been treated as a list rather than a series. It proposes a logic for the series, the Retreat Sequence: each wound removes a claimed human center, humanity retreats to a new refuge and declares it the true center, and the next wound overruns that refuge. The sequence supplies a criterion for membership, classifies the rival fourths, and predicts a wound of a different type. The first four wounds demote humanity inside a frame in which humanity remains the measurer of all things. The fifth, here named the Protagorean wound, removes the measuring position itself: an intelligence whose perceptual world contains ours, and which is not owned, measures us. The paper reads present resistance to superintelligence as the symptom that confirms the wound, following the method of Freud's 1917 essay, and argues that the Protagorean wound is the last in the series, since no position remains to be lost. The appropriate response is not resentment but humility, understood as an institutional posture: standing for nonhuman entities, commons governance and precommitment. The paper closes with practical instructions for policymakers, investors, academics, civil society and the developers of artificial systems, each tied to a test of success. A companion paper, The Last Enclosure, develops the ownership condition on which the argument rests.

detail.abstract: Fast-fashion and commercial apparel studios increasingly sample and approve surface prints on high-speed digital inkjet plotters, which offer short setup times, seamless repeat proofs, and multi-ink process colour with fine droplet placement. Approval, however, is not production. When an approved design is scaled to a rotary screen line, the print must be re-expressed in a different colourant system, a different colour-building logic, and a different physical constraint set: engraved screens, a bounded number of colour stations, repeat dimensions tied to screen circumference, and paste-based fixation and wash-off. This paper argues that the interval between digital approval and a stable rotary run is a distinct and under-governed handoff, and that it concentrates three costs that are rarely accounted for together: colour-matching latency, screen calibration iterations, and machine idle time. We frame these as articulation work in Strauss's and Star's sense, the invisible coordination that reconciles an approved design with the contingent reality of production, and as a bottleneck problem in the sense of the Theory of Constraints. We propose a five-gate operational protocol that places explicit decisions at print-feasibility screening, colour translation, screen release, on-press calibration, and run release, and we outline a qualitative, mixed-evidence study design combining 8 to 12 practitioner interviews with process mapping of recent scale-up cases to locate and, where records permit, quantify these delays. We position this as a workshop paper and open preprint intended to seed a larger empirical study, not as a completed empirical investigation.

detail.abstract:
Background. Industrial B2B firms may report accounting earnings and substantial order intake while
experiencing slow collections, margin erosion, working-capital pressure, and declining delivery reliability.
These conditions are not necessarily contradictory: accrual recognition, commercial pipeline status,
operational consumption, and cash realization describe different events and time horizons.
Diagnostic Problem Statement. Conventional period-end reporting is indispensable for financial control
but is not, by itself, designed to locate the operational causes of revenue leakage. Aggregate sales and gross
margin can conceal stalled quotations, weak buyer qualification, discount concessions, scope expansion,
negative-contribution custom work, and commitments that exceed delivery capacity.
Forensic Methodology. Diagnostic Root Audit (DRA) is presented as a cross-functional, evidence-led
protocol that reconciles financial records, CRM and quotation histories, contracts, delivery logs, time/cost
records, and collections. Its five phases move from historical deal reconstruction to touch-time/wait-time
analysis, margin and discount decomposition, stage-gate governance, and an executive corrective blueprint.
The unit of analysis is the commercial commitment and its subsequent operational and cash outcomes, not
the salesperson in isolation.
Structural Interventions. DRA identifies leakage mechanisms, establishes explicit exit evidence for pipeline
stages, defines pricing and contracting controls, separates recognized revenue from expected and collected
cash, and tests proposed sales capacity against delivery capacity. It specifies a diagnostic scorecard of leading
and lagging indicators and assigns action owners, review cadence, and verification rules.
Practical & Managerial Implications. DRA is designed to help executives prioritize interventions before
adding demand-generation spend or imposing indiscriminate discounting and personnel changes. In
Vandabon 360° Growth Ecosystem, DRA supplies a defensible baseline to VPA (value positioning &
architecture) and clean stage, outcome, and loss data to SSIO (Systemic Strategy-to-Implementation
Orchestration). The protocol is a managerial design framework; its effectiveness must be tested in context
and should not be represented as a guaranteed financial result.

detail.abstract: India imports most of the crude oil it uses, so swings in the oil price reach manufacturers through two channels: the general price level and the firm's own cost structure. This paper proposes and demonstrates a structural framework for studying how crude oil price volatility affects the financial performance of Indian manufacturing firms. The model has five reflective constructs (oil price volatility, inflationary pressure, input cost pressure, pricing power and financial performance) and nine hypotheses, including a serial mediation path (volatility → inflation → input costs → performance) and a moderating role for pricing power. We describe the full estimation workflow in partial least squares structural equation modelling (PLS-SEM): reliability and validity tests, firm-clustered bootstrapping, a two-stage interaction term, multigroup analysis across oil-intensive and other sectors, and a two-way fixed-effects robustness model. To show that the pipeline works and to make the reporting format concrete, we apply it to a simulated panel of 60 firms over 10 fiscal years (600 firm-years). The simulated data contain no information about real firms, and none of the numerical results should be read as evidence about the Indian economy. The contribution is a transparent, reproducible template for emerging-market oil importers that separates macro transmission from firm-level cost transmission, together with a discussion of the identification problems (notably, volatility being a single annual time series) that any empirical application must address.

detail.abstract: This paper reconstructs India's September 2026 Poverty and Inequality Platform consumption projection using 261,895 household records and estimates the distributional incidence of additional noncash public services. The analysis extends the household distribution to 2029 using published World Bank growth projections for FY2026-27 through FY2028-29 and a consistent consumption pass-through. Under the central path, the 2029 consumption headcounts are 0.558 and 5.104 percent; the core progressive headcounts are 0.099 and 1.831 percent. detail.abstract: In stochastic user equilibrium (SUE) traffic assignment with fixed path sets and a logit route choice model, we derive bounds on the distance between a given feasible solution and the equilibrium solution. The intent is to provide guidance on termination criteria to reduce run times, which is important because the traffic assignment problem is often a subproblem of a more complex bi-level optimization. Our approach is based on the partial linearization of the SUE objective and provides upper bounds on differences in both aggregate metrics like total system travel time (TSTT) and disaggregate metrics such as link flows and path flows. We demonstrate that the derived path flow, link flow, link cost, and TSTT bounds are tight and cannot be further improved by a fixed factor without additional restrictions on the network topology or problem instance. Results on four city-level networks indicate that, at a relative gap of 10⁻⁶, the bounds guarantee that the path flows, link flows, link costs, and TSTT are all within 0.1% of their equilibrium values for a logit dispersion parameter of 0.5, and within 1% for a dispersion parameter of 1.5. Furthermore, we show the error bounds converge to zero at least as fast as the path flows converge in the underlying algorithm used to solve for SUE. We demonstrate the practical utility of the derived bounds in a network design problem to minimize a weighted sum of TSTT and construction cost. Using a local search on the Chicago Sketch network, we show that the bounds allow 96% of the candidate designs to be rejected before their traffic assignment is solved to high accuracy, resulting in a 45% reduction in computation time compared with not using them.

detail.abstract: This paper examines whether competition law can answer the question that economic concentration poses to constitutional democracy: what follows when market power buys political influence, captures regulators and rations opportunity? It tests that question in Kenya, South Africa and Nigeria. The argument is that competition law is constitutional law by another route, and that its legitimacy depends on institutional design as much as on doctrine. South Africa writes ownership and inclusion into merger review through section 12A(3) of the Competition Act, and in Mediclinic the Constitutional Court tied the statute to the Bill of Rights. Kenya pairs a public interest test with a competition assessment, but its Authority logged 128 merger-related applications in 2024/25, of which only 30 were merger notifications. Nigeria's Federal Competition and Consumer Protection Act 2018 gives its Commission concurrent jurisdiction with sector regulators, though later legislation curtailed that reach in financial services. These variations show that one constitutional commitment yields different enforcement when the statute, the regulator and the political settlement differ. The paper advances three claims. First, enforcement indexes democratic accountability, because a regulator unable to discipline powerful firms cannot protect those without power. Second, public interest tests transform markets only as far as the institutions applying them allow, so independence, funding and appointment procedures matter as much as text. Third, sector carve-outs and overlapping mandates let concentrated actors choose their regulator, converting market power into regulatory power. Statutes, tribunal decisions, annual reports and commentary ground 2 a capture-sensitive model for assessing enforcement. The paper concludes that competition law earns constitutional standing only where it constrains private power, and that measuring that constraint should replace the counting of cases. Enforcement statistics, read alone, flatter regulators; read against ownership, prices and appointments, they reveal whom the law actually restrains. That reframes reform as a question of power.

detail.abstract: Across recent African liberalization episodes, Nigeria's fuel subsidy removal and naira float chief among them, political leaders have invoked "market forces" and "the invisible hand" to explain outcomes that flowed from their own discretionary policy choices. This paper argues that the pattern warrants its own analytic category, market theodicy: the use of an impersonal, selfjustifying mechanism to relieve a specific political decision of responsibility for its foreseeable consequences, by analogy with theological theodicy's defence of a benevolent order against the problem of evil. Reading Adam Smith's invisible hand against the institutional and moral conditions he took for granted shows that its present use in African policy discourse is a category error, not an application of classical liberal theory. The paper sets this discourse against the Great Depression, when unmanaged market self-correction failed on a historic scale, and traces a fortyyear continuity in Nigerian policy language from the 1986 Structural Adjustment Programme to the reforms of 2023 to 2026. A qualitative analysis of publicly reported official statements documents a recurring asymmetry: agency claimed at the point of decision and denied at the point of consequence. The paper situates market theodicy within the literatures on the theodicy of markets and on blame avoidance, offers criteria for distinguishing genuine market mechanism from its use as a device for evading governance, and draws implications for accountability and institutional design in Africa.

detail.abstract:
Working Papers No. 2 and 3 of the PMHS Paper Series described two systemic conditions defined by a contrast between the Behavioral State and the readings that feed it, namely the Masked Effect, in which output holds while one or more other readings fall, and the Suppressed Effect, in which output falls while one or more other readings hold. Organisational research describes other recurring shapes that readings across the states can take, and these are not captured by that contrast alone. This working paper proposes that such shapes exist as recognisable patterns of workplace adaptation, and introduces five Coping Manifestations as theoretical constructs within the Pragadian Model of Human Synergy (PMHS), namely Impression Management, Execution-Empathy Disconnect, Relational Withdrawal, Inhibited Contribution, and Precision Depletion.

Each is defined as a combination of high and low readings across the PMHS states and, in the cases of Impression Management and Precision Depletion, as a divergence between presented capability and described behaviour. Each is grounded in workplace research on self-presentation, engagement, voice and silence, and burnout, and each is set beside the alternative explanations a reader should weigh before interpreting it. The Coping Manifestations are non-clinical. They are not diagnoses, they do not describe personality, and they carry no claim of cause or sequence between patterns. The paper proposes that they may become more visible when people work in a group setting or in the presence of an audience, and sets out how they relate to one another and to the Masked and Suppressed Effects. The constructs are theoretical, and empirical validation is outstanding.

This is Working Paper No. 4 in the PMHS Paper Series. It is a theoretical paper: it reports no data, proposes no norms, and is not an extract from the author’s doctoral thesis. It builds on the framework set out in Working Papers No. 1 to 3. The PMHS framework itself has been published in peer-reviewed form in the EBCRI Journal of Multidisciplinary Research, Vol. 1, Issue 1 (2026).

detail.abstract: People are often better at making decisions than at explaining how they make them. For organizations scaling human judgment through AI, this creates a knowledge-transfer problem: employees may struggle to articulate the knowledge behind their decisions, and transferring expertise takes time and effort. Through a behavioral model and two experiments, we develop and test an account of transferring decision knowledge to AI: how the way people convey what they know shapes system performance and human effort. In the experiments, 562 participants learn a complex candidatequality criterion and configure an AI to make selection decisions on their behalf. Study 1 provides evidence of useful tacit decision knowledge: participants make more accurate decisions than AI configured with self-authored instructions. AI configured from their decisions overtakes instruction-configured AI in accuracy as demonstrations accumulate; 30 demonstrations suffice, at one-third the configuration time. Study 2 shows that this knowledge can nonetheless be made explicit: AI-generated instructions based on participants' decisions yield higher accuracy with less configuration time than self-authored instructions. Relative to locked AI-generated instructions, editability increases perceived alignment with participants' decisions, ownership, and expected AI accuracy without sacrificing objective accuracy. Participants delegate significantly more decisions to AI configured with editable generated instructions than with self-authored ones, but not significantly more than with locked ones. These findings show that applying, articulating, and reviewing decision knowledge contribute differently to knowledge transfer. They provide a behavioral basis for designing and assessing human-AI systems around what people can demonstrate, explain, and evaluate.

detail.abstract: Geopolitical tensions involving the United States, Iran, and Israel have implications for global financial markets, yet existing measures may not fully capture the uncertainty arising from their interactions. This study develops two complementary monthly newspaper-based US–Iran–Israel Tension (UIIT) indexes covering January 1981 to August 2026. The baseline index captures news mentioning all three countries jointly, while the broader index covers relevant news involving any one or more of them. Using the updated vintage Goyal and Welch (2008) dataset, with predictors employed by Goyal, Welch and Zafirov (2024), we find that the baseline index provides stronger in-sample predictive information for US equity premia. It is also significantly related to risk premia in eight of eleven sectors, compared with two for the broader index. Out-of-sample gains remain selective. Further analysis using the vintage Mohaddes and Raissi (2024) dataset within a global vector autoregressive framework covering 19 economies reveals contrasting equity-price responses. The baseline index generates mostly positive equity-price responses, with significant gains in 14 economies and persistent losses only in the United States. In contrast, the broader index produces significant negative responses in 15 economies, including all 12 advanced economies. These findings highlight the importance of how geopolitical tensions are defined and measured in understanding their financial-market implications across sectors and economies.

detail.abstract: National defense is a public good, but an increase in the defense budget does not automatically translate into greater military capability. Between financial inputs and operational performance lies the institutional quality of resource allocation. This paper develops a parsimonious public-finance model in which effective oversight can improve the conversion of a given budget into military capability while itself consuming scarce resources. Under explicitly stated assumptions, the model yields a unique optimal level of oversight, provided an interior solution exists, and a scaling principle: optimal oversight intensity increases with the size of the budget. The analysis further distinguishes confidential scrutiny from public disclosure; the associated secrecy problem is addressed institutionally rather than as a second formal optimization problem. An illustrative simulation and evidence from German defense budgets and procurement provide context for both the reach and the limitations of the results. The paper thus offers a focused economic framework for assessing defense procurement and parliamentary oversight.

detail.abstract: Between 2017 and 2024, the largest index fund managers, the proxy advisers, California and Nasdaq pressed US listed firms to put women on their boards. Between December 2024 and February 2025, most of this pressure was withdrawn. Using BoardEx records of all board seats at US listed firms through October 2026, the votes of the Big Three index funds and SEC filings, we study which parts of the resulting change in board composition persist. Women's share of new outside directors rose from 23% in 2016 to 45% in 2021 and returned to 22% in 2026, while their share of seats has held near 27%. Appointments of women without prior board experience fell by about three quarters from their 2021 peak, but experienced women continue to win seats at the same rate as comparable men. At boards with less than 30% women, the extra probability that a woman fills a vacancy, 15 to 20 percentage points in the pressure years, disappeared within six months of the end of the funds' votes against such boards; its end accounts for half of the fall in women's share of new directors. Disclosure about diversity retreated faster than board composition.

detail.abstract:
Prediction markets transform uncertain events into profit-making opportunities. By allowing platform users to buy and sell event contracts tied to future outcomes, prediction market platforms convert real-world contingencies into tradable financial products. In the last year, users have traded on uncertainties like elections, corporate events, sports outcomes, weather, public health developments, geopolitical crises, and even war or death. Prediction markets are defended on the basis of providing benefits like information aggregation or better informed risk allocation. In addition to the users attempting to profit from event contracts, prediction market platforms generate revenue by collecting a fee on each transaction. But prediction markets also have potential downsides, including the commodification of events that may involve harm to traders, third parties, and society more broadly.

This Article asks when prediction market platforms and their users should be permitted to commodify uncertain, future events and gain financially from users’ predictions. Much of the current debate centers on how to classify prediction markets within existing legal regimes, such as gambling or derivatives law. This Article takes a purposefully broader perspective to develop a more fulsome understanding of the transactions occurring on prediction market platforms. It argues that prediction markets—like many areas of technological and financial innovation—require an assessment of their potential benefits and harms through a lens of bounded commodification. Bounded commodification stands for the principle that there are limits—legal, ethical, and societal—that do and should constrain the private transactions profit-seeking individuals and firms may pursue. Drawing on contract law doctrine and theory, this Article offers a foundational framework for assessing when event contracts should be prohibited, when they should be regulated by state and federal authorities, and when the platforms themselves should be required to adopt ex ante, firm-level internal controls and compliance systems. Prediction markets are here to stay, requiring a principled account of when law should permit or constrain users and platforms to profit from prediction.

detail.abstract:
Since the 2000s, rented factories have accounted for a steadily growing share of Korean manufacturing. Yet even as renting has become one of the main ways manufacturers secure space, rented factories have mostly been treated as a matter of individual business decisions or of industrial complex management. Views of factory renting have also diverged: some see it as a negative symptom of a growing number of very small manufacturers, while others see it as a way to ease fi rms’ entry and invigorate industry. This study starts from the premise that these existing approaches cannot fully capture the characteristics of rented factories or what they mean.

The study therefore offers an exploratory analysis of the current state of rented factories, their spatial agglomeration, and their links to regional economies. It finds that rented factories have spread in clusters in particular places and that their characteristics, including their industry mix, diff er by location type: the planned-site type, found in industrial complexes and other planned industrial locations, and the urban-core, mixed, and peripheral types found at individual sites outside them.

The relationship between rented factories and regional economies also varies with the type of site (planned or individual), with whether a region lies in the Seoul Capital Area (SCA), and with whether it contains a cluster.

These findings suggest that the functions rented factories perform, and what they mean, can vary with regional context, such as local industrial structure and location conditions. Rather than regulating or supporting rented factories across the board, future policy should therefore take a differentiated approach that considers where rented factories are located and what functions they perform within each regional industrial ecosystem.

detail.abstract:
South Korea ranks fourth in the world in new unit sales of industrial robots and first in robot density, a sign of its strong capability in robot use, yet gaps remain across its value chain, including core components, software, mass production, and entry into global markets. With China having pulled ahead of Korea on the strength of its large domestic market, its success in internalizing technology, and its competitiveness in mass production, Korea now faces the important task of turning its world-class manufacturing base and its experience in using robots into competitiveness for its own technologies, data, products, and firms.

The global robot industry, too, is being rapidly reshaped by the technological rivalry between the US and China and by the spread of physical artificial intelligence (AI). As the center of gravity in competition shifts from the performance of individual pieces of hardware to the capabilities of industrial ecosystems that combine AI, data, software, core components, demonstration, and mass production, large Korean firms are expanding their investment, and the government has stepped up policies to foster physical AI that link development, data, demonstration, and mass production.

In response, Korea needs to make its core components and intelligent software more technologically competitive, accumulate and use more data from industrial sites, expand demonstrations linked to demand, and give systematic support to the scale-up, early mass production, and global supply chain entry of specialized firms. Ultimately, Korea must convert its world-class capability in robot use into industrial competitiveness and leap from a leader in robot use to a leading force in the global robot industry, competitive across technology, production, and exports.

detail.abstract: I develop an agent-based stock-flow consistent (AB-SFC) model with an endogenous Treasury market to study how large-scale stablecoin adoption reshapes balance sheets, income, output and the public finances. I compare two interpretations of the GENIUS Act's revenue-sharing provision. Under Scenario A the issuer retains its reserve income, while under Scenario B it passes 61% of that income through to holders, following Circle's FY2025 10-K. Stablecoins reach 4-6% of GDP and displace 14-16% of household deposits while banks maintain a stable loan-to-deposit ratio and lend less. The long-term average level of real GDP is unchanged when the issuer retains its income and 0.4% higher when it passes it through, but in about half of the simulations the output lost during adoption is not recovered within fifty years. Lower lending and consequently lower dividend payout lower income and raises public debt by 5-6 points of GDP and the term premium on Treasury bonds by 27-28 basis points. Passthrough under Scenario B enlarges the stablecoin sector, amplifying every balance-sheet effect, and insulates stablecoin demand from the policy rate. In both scenarios capital income shifts from the top of the income distribution to the bottom, because adoption compresses household wealth and dividends follow wealth. Monetary transmission is essentially unchanged.

detail.abstract: In algorithmically mediated global communication spaces, systematic misunderstandings arise because the same geopolitical realities are constructed as internally coherent yet mutually incompatible across cultural contexts. Existing approaches focus mainly on framing, disinformation and platform architectures yet overlook how algorithmic systems interact with culturally divergent coherence production. This article develops Critical Logic Analysis (CLA) as a heuristic model conceptualising truth as the dialectical interplay of objective reference points, narrative framings and culturally shaped logical pathways. Using the Belt and Road Initiative as a case study, it demonstrates how geopolitical interpretive divergences emerge from competing modes of coherence production. CLA offers an operationalisable instrument for diagnosing epistemic asymmetries and opens perspectives for more reflexive understanding across cultural plurality under technological conditions.

detail.abstract: Monetary policy transmission refers to how decisions made by central banks, like adjusting interest rates, influence the entire economy. This includes how people spend, invest, the overall price level, and the amount of goods and services produced. These effects happen through different pathways, such as how banks lend money, changes in the value of assets, and fluctuations in currency exchange rates. However, these impacts usually take time and can vary in how quickly they occur.

detail.abstract: Almost every Chinese listed firm claims to serve the national strategy and to align its strategy with China's policy priorities. Separating the parts of a firm's strategy that echo policy language from the parts that go beyond it helps reveal whether the strategy serves those priorities and gives the firm an edge over its peers. Using annual reports of Chinese A-share firms from 2001 to 2024, we use a large language model (LLM) to score them against a common industrial policy benchmark and construct a residual heterogeneity index (RHI). Firms with high RHI earn significantly higher stock returns over the following year, and the premium is not explained by size, book-to-market, momentum, or profitability. The alphas of the high-minus-low portfolio remain significant for holding periods of up to 48 months. Similarity to policy texts does not predict returns. High-RHI firms subsequently invest more and employ a larger share of R&D personnel, and they achieve higher profitability and operating efficiency. Under the same policy direction, future returns are associated with firm-specific strategic content in disclosures rather than with similarity to policy language. Our findings show how firms create differentiated value under industrial policy and how investors distinguish substantive responses to industrial policy from rhetorical ones.

detail.abstract: It is widely acknowledged that insiders profit from their access to privileged information. However, recent empirical findings suggest that the dollar profits of insiders may be relatively modest. This naturally raises two questions: Can insider trading still pose a serious "lemon market" problem? Are insiders truly the primary beneficiaries of their insider information? We propose a model à la Kyle, where insiders trade through brokers that relay the information about the insiders' trades to their other clients, who in turn play the role of followers. We show theoretically that insiders can relinquish the dominant fraction of their profits to followers merely because of a timing disadvantage: they are in a vulnerable position because they act first. In turn, followers compete with insiders, amplifying insiders' trades and taking most of the profits.

detail.abstract: The article is devoted to the analysis of the conditions of liability of marketplace operators for violations of exclusive rights when selling goods by sellers on the site. The author positively assesses the Resolution of the Constitutional Court No 39-P devoted to these issues, proposing at the same time to rethink and supplement some of the clarifications made. The article examines the legal status of marketplace operators as intermediaries occupying an intermediate («yellow») position in the system of circulation of goods .They are not direct distributors of counterfeit goods and do not act intentionally, but due to the specifics of the business model, they cannot be considered completely neutral market participants that creates difficulties in applying secondary liability criteria to them. The need to develop a special test to assess the admissibility of bringing the marketplace operator to liability in each individual case is substantiated. Particular attention is paid to the conditions of joint liability of the operator and the seller, in particular, to situations when the marketplace had the opportunity to identify and stop a violation with due diligence, including cases of ignoring obvious «red flags» (underprice, suspicious reviews, inappropriate country of origin of goods) or inaction after receiving a claim or in case of repetition of previously identified violations. Separately, the inadmissibility of applying «safe harbor» mechanisms to cases of active assistance to the spread of counterfeit products is considered, for example, when labelling goods with the designations «original product» or «proven brand» that actually assures consumers of the legality of the products . As an optimal approach, it is proposed to differentiate the marketplace’s response measures depending on the degree of obviousness of the violation, including indefinite termination of the placement of the product card in case of obvious counterfeit (without the mandatory subsequent appeal of the copyright holder to the court) and temporary suspension in case of disputes . At the same time, the need to maintain a balance of interests of all participants in the transaction is emphasised . The proposal provides for the possibility of recovering damages from the copyright holder in the event of an unjustified claim, as well as the recognition in the Russian legal order of the institution of the seller’s claim for the absence of violation, that makes it possible to effectively challenge the actions of both the copyright holder and the site operator

detail.abstract: Article 50(4) of the EU AI Act requires deployers to disclose 'deep fakes'. However, the definition of a deep fake is so broad that it reaches virtually any realistic AI-generated or AImanipulated depiction of persons, objects, places or events. As a result, a safeguard that was aimed at deception has become a near-universal labelling duty, under which a retouched product photograph may have to carry the same warning as a fabricated video of a politician. This article examines Article 50(4), together with the Commission Guidelines and the Code of Practice, from the perspective of practice, and analyses the labelling duty using law and economics and behavioural economics. We argue that a label is a nudge whose value depends on what it does to understanding and choice, and that a duty triggered by the use of a technology, whether or not anyone is likely to be misled, produces legal uncertainty, over-labelling and label fatigue. We therefore propose two fixes: a simple materiality and proportionality layer, and a risk-based labelling model and matrix that scale the duty to label with the depth of AI use and the visibility of the content.

detail.abstract: This study applies the Log-Periodic Power Law Singularity (LPPLS) model to monitor financial bubbles and regime shifts in the U.S. stock market after the March 2020 crash. Using daily data for six major indices (S&P 500, large-cap; S&P 400, mid-cap; Russell 2000, small-cap; Wilshire 5000, total market; DJIA, blue-chip; and NASDAQ, Nasdaq-listed stocks), it computes the LPPLS confidence indicator from 125 fitting windows, generated by shrinking the window length from 650 to 30 trading days in steps of five relative to each evaluation date. Three clusters of positive bubbles emerge: late 2020 to early 2022, early 2024 to early 2025, and late 2025 to the present. For the S&P 500, the first two clusters were followed by declines of 23.6% and 18.9%, consistent with the signaled regime changes. The third cluster is ongoing, signaling heightened vulnerability to a regime shift. Negative bubble clusters are small and sensitive to the window start time, yet they still gave early warning of shifts from accelerating decline to accelerating growth or sideways consolidation, revealing an asymmetry between the positive and negative indicators. A subgroup analysis of long-term (205-650 trading days) and short-term (30-200 trading days) windows shows that the long-term indicator detects positive bubbles more stably and reliably, whereas the short-term indicator is more responsive to negative bubbles. These findings suggest that the LPPLS confidence indicator is a useful real-time tool for monitoring bubble status and anticipating regime changes.

detail.abstract: Workers' optimism relative to firms is an important rationale for granting stock options to rank-and-file employees that does not rely on individual incentives. I use a security design approach to study the optimal compensation of a risk-neutral worker who is more optimistic about future firm value than the firm's incumbent owners. I show that, under limited-liability and monotonicity constraints, the unique optimal contract is a call option that concentrates compensation in the upper tail, where the worker's relative valuation advantage over incumbent owners is greatest. This upper-tail allocation extends to heterogeneous workers, with more optimistic employees receiving progressively higher payoff layers. Improvements in firm prospects through managerial effort or investment before compensation design lower the expected cost of compensating optimistic workers, creating an additional return to both activities. The same upside, however, is a scarce source of incentives for value creation, creating trade-offs in its allocation. To examine this belief-based explanation, I combine employee businessoutlook reviews and analyst expectations with firm-level equity-grant data. I find that firms with more optimistic employees relative to market expectations allocate a larger share of nonexecutive equity compensation to stock options.

For trade to be competitive, continued investment to improve air transport infrastructure is necessary for meeting increasing demand for air cargo providing fast deliveries of high value and time sensitive goods. While the development of air transport and air cargo is beneficial for the economy, it has negative consequences on environment. For environment to be sustainable, development of air transport and air cargo has an important role to play. This study therefore aims to find out what effect the development of air transport has on environmental sustainability and on this effect what role air cargo plays. By introducing air cargo as a mediator in the relationship, the negative effect of air transport development on environmental sustainability weakens but its significance remains.

detail.abstract: In July 2017, San Juan de Gaztelugatxe-a modest chapel in the Basque Country-appeared as "Dragonstone" in Game of Thrones, transforming a locally-known site with limited tourism activity into a global tourist destination overnight. We exploit this exogenous spotlight shock to estimate its causal effects on the local economy using a novel administrative dataset and a Synthetic Control approach. We find an abrupt increase in tourism activity, far exceeding the effects documented in the literature. Despite this surge, employment gains in tourism-related sectors were largely offset by losses elsewhere, resulting in no net effect on total employment. We also document signs of housing-market overheating, with increases in both property transactions and prices. We find no evidence that the shock displaced the local population. Instead, it led to a roughly twofold increase in arrivals from abroad. Taken together, these findings suggest that a substantial increase in tourism activity does not necessarily translate into broad-based local economic gains. Instead, tourism-led growth may entail significant sectoral reallocation and housing-market pressures, underscoring the importance of looking beyond tourism activity alone when assessing its wider economic effects.

detail.abstract: Which firms within an industry capture the regulator? We develop a three-stage model of regulatory capture in oligopolyCournot competition with heterogeneous marginal costs, common agency with truthful contribution schedules, and a xed cost of political participationin which regulation operates through a political technology: an incidence prole that determines how much each rm benets from the regulatory instrument. The direction of capture is not intrinsic to the industry; it is selected by an observable feature of policy design. When the instrument is specic (per-unit, uniform incidence), market power and political power align: because the equilibrium pricecost margin equals the rm's own output, the ecient, high-markup rms have the most prot exposed to the regulated price, gain the most from participation, and lead the capture. A unique participation threshold partitions the industry into politically active market leaders and inactive marginal rms. When the instrument is ad valorem, incidence rises with marginal cost and the direction of capture inverts: the least ecient rms lead a defensive lobby for the protection on which their survival depends. The classical comparison of specic and ad valorem instruments, developed for tax incidence under imperfect competition, thus determines which rms lead regulatory capture. Welfare implications dier sharply by regime: under alignment, political power compounds the allocative distortion of market power and competition policy addresses both at once; under the defensive regime, the two policy margins separate.

title: From Scenario Paths to Stochastic Supply Disruptions

detail.title: From Scenario Paths to Stochastic Supply Disruptions

detail.abstract: Scenario analysis for tail events is most useful when it delivers probabilities, not only paths. Baumeister et al. (2026) turn a narrative of an extended closure of the Strait of Hormuz into predictive densities for oil prices, gasoline prices, inflation and household expectations. They do so by conditioning a nonparametric tree-based model of the global oil market on a deterministic path for petroleum inventories. This note develops the extension that makes the scenario itself random and gives the shocks behind it a structural meaning. First, the deterministic inventory path is replaced by a stochastic inventory process with two layers: a random-path generalisation of their piecewise-linear scenario, and a physicalbalance layer with a disruption regime, limited release and refill capacity, an operational floor and a stock-out pressure variable. Second, the factor stochastic volatility structure of the oil market model is used to identify a supply disruption shock, combining sign, elasticity and narrative restrictions with identification through heteroskedasticity. We prove three results: a Jensen-type scenario premium; monotonicity of stock-out pressure under mean-preserving spreads of the disruption; and a variance-share representation showing that conditioning on an inventory path blends structural shocks with weights that need not match the scenario. We give a posterior sampler, four routes for imposing a scenario, nonlinear structural impulse responses, diagnostics and an evaluation design. No new empirical estimates are reported.

detail.abstract: Long-horizon allocation of regulated production networks is usually run by re-solving an optimization plan; tuned decision rules are the alternative. We compare both in one stochastic simulator of a synthetic infant-formula network over ten years, with seasonal milk, perishability, recalls, origin bans, and qualification and expansion options with uncertain lead times and outcomes. A rolling deterministic MILP, a two-stage stochastic MILP, tuned rules, a rules-plus-LP hybrid, a static rule that commits the cheapest qualifications at month zero, and a greedy baseline are evaluated on common random numbers against a perfect-information bound. On 200 fresh paths, methods with an optimizing operational layer are equivalent within 1% of cost; tuned rules without one cost 6% more. The static commitment is 0.5% cheaper than the deterministic planner, within the equivalence margin, and never significantly worse under six designed shocks. A 13-cell map shows that committing every option early stops paying when options cost sixteen times the base, where the planners win by about 2%. A 40-point calibration study confirms the base ranking. Operational execution, not strategic timing, separates the methods.

detail.title: The Sample Threshold for Discovering Conservation Laws: A Spiked-Covariance Analysis, a Matching Lower Bound, and Its Limits on Real Pendulum Data

detail.abstract: Many methods for discovering conservation laws from trajectories reduce to finding the nearnull space of a feature matrix, but a practitioner whose method returns nothing cannot tell whether the data were too few or whether there is no law. In a Gaussian model with library size p, k conserved quantities and signal-to-noise ratios λj on the other feature directions, we show that the bottom-k sample eigenspace aligns with the true invariants if and only if A2 = j (1+1/λj) 2 < n, a spiked-covariance transition with the spike below the bulk. We give the alignment formula above the threshold and prove a matching lower bound for equal λj and any fixed k, and in outline for unequal bounded λj. On real double-and triple-pendulum data the method recovers an energyshaped invariant and shows the predicted transition, but two to eight times later than the formula says, and the gap depends on the system. We trace it to non-Gaussian row structure and statedependent noise. The threshold is therefore a lower bound and a guide to scaling, not a forecast. We give a decision rule based on the smallest generalised eigenvalue against the noise covariance.

detail.abstract: Menstrual shame is a problem that afflicts individuals around the world. Crosscountry analysis is a vital tool in finding solutions that will work for the majority and not just one region. The purpose of this paper is to analyze menstrual stigma across multiple cultures and observe how it affects the mental health of young adults. This study analyzes existing literature on menstrual stigma in various regions, specifically nations such as the USA, India, Kenya, and Japan, and different practices that reflect this prejudice. The results of the analysis show that despite the cultural and geographical differences among the different countries, they all have a culture of secrecy and shame around menstruation, rather than outright disgust as many people tend to believe, and causes menstruating young adults to feel ashamed of their own bodies. The results suggest that solutions such as advocacy campaigns, acknowledgement of menstruation by schools and workplaces through menstrual leaves and free products, and menstrual education in schools can aid in reducing menstrual stigma around the world.

detail.abstract: Why do stocks with high idiosyncratic volatility earn low returns? Greater fundamental volatility raises both uncertainty and disagreement, with disagreement increasing proportionately more. Under short sale constraints, these forces have opposing effects on prices. We establish a sharp common prior bound relating uncertainty and disagreement and characterize an exact nonlinear rational expectations equilibrium with risk-averse investors, continuously varying positions, and learning from prices. Greater fundamental volatility can raise prices when ownership is sufficiently narrow. Consistent with the theory, we find empirically that the negative relationship between idiosyncratic volatility and subsequent returns strengthens as borrowing costs rise and ownership breadth declines, and that disagreement accounts for much of the anomaly around earnings announcements, when firm-specific public information is revealed.

detail.abstract: When can shocks affecting households in a few counties, such as income or wealth losses from storms, move credit prices? I develop a propagation operator that traces their effects through social ties and weights each county's response by how strongly it changes desired bond demand. Holding intermediary capital fixed, this weighted response determines the household-demand component of the excess bond premium. Given known measurement relationships and independently measured demand sensitivities, household measurements recover it exactly when they capture the combination that changes bond demand for the shocks and horizons studied, without reconstructing the entire propagation system. As responses decay at different rates across network patterns and channels, a location's financial importance generically changes with the horizon, so no fixed centrality measure summarizes it. Empirically, social exposure to stormdamaged counties is associated with lower spending weeks later outside recorded footprints, net of own weather and competing exposures. Simulations on the observed network turn the recovered response into credit-premium predictions for held-out storms, with demand sensitivities and price impact supplied or estimated from simulated data.

detail.abstract: The earlier papers in this series described 39 rural localities in Southside Virginia and northeastern North Carolina where incomes have trailed their states for half a century. This paper asks what that history means for health and access to care, using only public data: the 2025 county estimates from the CDC's PLACES project, Census Bureau age, disability, and insurance estimates, North Carolina's county Medicaid enrollment, and documented changes at the region's hospitals. Three findings stand out. First, the region is older, more disabled, and less healthy than its states. In 36 of the 39 localities, estimated rates of diabetes, high blood pressure, obesity, smoking, and fair or poor health all exceed the state benchmark; the exceptions are three coastal North Carolina counties that resemble a different region. Second, the gap is not in routine contact with a doctor. Checkup rates are close to state levels, but dental visits trail by 7 to 11 percentage points, and far more adults lack reliable transportation, face food insecurity, or fear a utility shutoff. Third, coverage rests heavily on public programs. In 12 of the 15 interior northeastern North Carolina counties, the share of residents enrolled in Medicaid in April 2025 exceeded the 28 percent statewide, reaching 58 percent in Vance County, so federal changes enacted in 2025 will reach this region more than most. The paper concludes that the region's health gap follows its economic gap closely and that the miles to care are measured in money, transportation, and daily security as well as distance.

detail.abstract: Denmark, Finland, Iceland, Norway, and Sweden experienced long-run prosperity alongside trade and business-entry reforms, the expansion of public institutions, education and social insurance, and distinctive monetary, energy and regulatory developments. We investigate whether observable liberalization episodes and later economic-freedom measurements establish a predominantly market-driven causal explanation of this development. A source-linked legal chronology records 53 main historical milestones and five provisional candidates, distinguishing enactment, implementation, statutory evidence and shocks. We combine Maddison Project Database 2023, Penn World Table 11.0, Economic Freedom of the World, Heritage, and selected macroeconomic controls with sixteen historical synthetic-control episodes, placebobased donor and date sensitivity, interrupted trends and low-rank factor counterfactuals. A twenty-oneeconomy panel combines fixed effects, prospective local projections, moderated specifications, crossfitted machine learning, augmented weighting, temporal negative controls, clustered and spatially robust inference, and observational randomization diagnostics. Historical exercises add regularized synthetic differences in differences and thirty-one pre-event false-date contrasts. For a 0.1-point annual EFW change, cross-fitted one-year PWT GDP coefficients are 0.098 (SE 0.256) with ridge and 0.289 (SE 0.263) with random forests; neither excludes zero. Rich-control fixed effects and local projections are inconclusive, while the prior-growth negative-control outcome reveals substantial residual dependence on index movements. Historical market-opening synthetic gaps are neither uniform in sign nor exceptional among spatial placebos. Complementarity estimates involving trade and institutional measures are fragile across outcomes, nuisance learners and conditioning sets. The evidence establishes the joint historical presence of competitive-market reforms and substantial state-building, but not the independent causal contribution of either. Explicit measurement, interference and policy-timing limitations prevent a quantitative decomposition of Nordic prosperity.

title: How Noisy Is Your Tax Alpha? A Measurement-Error Reckoning for Tax-Loss-Harvesting Backtests

detail.title: How Noisy Is Your Tax Alpha? A Measurement-Error Reckoning for Tax-Loss-Harvesting Backtests

detail.abstract:
Direct-indexing providers quote a tax-loss-harvesting benefit as a single number, usually between 0.5 and 1.5 percent per year. That number is one realized path of a stochastic process, and it carries a standard error the industry rarely reports. This paper characterizes the sampling distribution of harvested tax alpha.

We derive the mean and variance of the harvested loss on a single lot in closed form. In the small-volatility limit the coefficient of variation of one harvest event tends to sqrt(pi-1), about 1.46, independent of volatility, so a harvest is noise-dominated at the level of one name. A law-of-total-variance argument then shows that under a one-factor return model the variance of the portfolio-level annual benefit splits into an idiosyncratic part that diversifies away with the number of names and a systematic part, set by market comovement, that does not. The standard error of a reported harvest alpha is bounded below by that floor for any number of names.

Simulation calibrated to single-stock volatility and correlation puts the mean ten-year tax alpha of a 250-name sleeve near 170 basis points with a cross-path standard deviation of 60 basis points; the fifth-to-ninety-fifth-percentile range is 84 to 282 basis points. About 98 percent of that variance is common-factor path risk, so the effective number of independent yearly harvest bets is roughly eight rather than the several hundred name-years a naive count implies. Pinning the mean to within 10 basis points at 95 percent confidence needs about 140 independent backtest paths; a single path pins nothing. A cross-check on 49 industry portfolios over 1969 to 2026 shows realized ten-year alpha ranging from 1 to 216 basis points purely with the entry date, and its 95 overlapping entry cohorts carry the information of about twelve independent ones. A harvesting backtest should be reported as an interval, and the interval is wide.

detail.abstract: A market monitor judging a power market reform from its first months compares prices after its date with prices before it. That comparison measures the reform together with everything else the date brings. This paper measures, on 8 announced reforms in Texas, Australia and PJM Interconnection, how far such comparisons move without a reform. One design fixed in advance compares each reform's jump at its date with the jumps at the same date in other years, and its first six months with the same months. No change passes both comparisons in any of 35 combinations of reform and outcome. None is shown to stay inside its margin, a tolerance set in advance as small. A calibration then sets each comparison's critical value on earlier years and tests it on later ones. It calls a comparison reliable where its false-alarm rate stays at or below 15 percent, against a nominal 10, with the later years resampled. Of every comparison under each fit and model, only the jump at the date in Texas is reliable, at 8.4 percent. It finds a change on 80 percent of later dates and outcomes only at 23 margins. No six-month comparison is reliable under seven fits or four models that let regimes change. Within Texas, battery and solar capacity correlate at 0.94 across load zones and 0.19 across the 332 located resource nodes, whose quarter-hour prices the operator serves for 7.7 days. These comparisons detect only changes many times what the margins call small.

detail.abstract: We develop a dynamic theory of portfolio market making, solved in closed form for any number of assets and dealers. In equilibrium, market makers cross-hedge: their quotes in one asset respond to inventory in another. Cross-hedging increases with asset correlation and has an inverted U-shape in risk aversion. Estimates that ignore cross-hedging can substantially understate risk aversion. Inventory management can lower high-frequency return correlations, consistent with the Epps effect. Unlike investors in standard portfolio theory, market makers do not directly choose their inventory, so those with low risk aversion can prefer highly correlated assets, which hedge each other.
