detail.abstract: China's exceptional export surplus need not signal strong domestic demand. This paper argues that, after a housing-credit bust, weak domestic absorption can contribute to a trade surplus: constrained borrowers deleverage while savers accumulate claims, and a managed exchange rate limits adjustment through nominal depreciation. With downward nominal wage rigidity, firms may clear excess capacity abroad by compressing export prices and margins. The model shows how rising export volumes can coexist with weak domestic sales and lower export unit values, while distinguishing this mechanism from capacity expansion, import compression, and genuine cost advantages. The surplus generated by the model is cyclical deferred absorption, not a complete explanation of China's persistent external surplus. Exploratory evidence from Chinese industries and listed firms is consistent with margin pressure in housing-exposed manufacturing, but does not show a shift from domestic to overseas sales. Product-level evidence finds no broad-based increase in export unit values after the 2025 anti-involution campaign. The evidence therefore does not establish that weak demand caused China's surplus or quantify its contribution. Its primary contribution is a micro-founded diagnostic framework that separates demand diversion from capacity expansion, import compression, and cost-led competitiveness. detail.abstract: The rapid development of the digital economy, blockchain technology, and decentralized identity is reshaping the traditional role of banks within the economy. This study proposes an NDAChain-enabled banking model in which banks are repositioned as Trust Anchors, providing digital identity services, information attestation, data verification, and trusted data-sharing services within the digital ecosystem. Drawing upon financial intermediation theory, digital trust theory, and decentralized identity frameworks, the study adopts a conceptual research approach supported by a literature review of blockchain technology, digital trust infrastructure, and digital financial services to develop the proposed model. The findings suggest that NDAChain can enable banks to expand their role from traditional financial intermediaries to trust intermediaries that facilitate identity verification and trust connectivity among citizens, businesses, government agencies, and digital service providers. From a theoretical perspective, the study extends the scope of financial intermediation theory into the domain of digital trust within the digital economy. From a practical perspective, the proposed model can reduce information verification costs, enhance trusted data sharing, foster innovation in financial services, and contribute to the development of a national digital trust infrastructure that supports digital transformation and sustainable digital economic growth.

detail.abstract: The price of cash-flow risk rises when professional forecasters fear a recession, whether or not consumption has fallen. Past consumption and unemployment explain only 12% of this fear, which sets it apart from the consumption history behind habit models. detail.abstract: New Zealand's 1984 withdrawal of agricultural support is the standard reference case for agricultural liberalization, and it is generally read as evidence that removing subsidies raises productivity. That reading rests on before-and-after comparisons rather than on an explicit counterfactual. I build synthetic controls for New Zealand from ten structurally comparable economies that did not reform over the same window, and estimate the effect of the post-1984 reform package on aggregate agricultural total factor productivity and on four measures of sectoral composition between 1984 and 1994. I find no detectable effect on total factor productivity. Instead, I find a recompision of output. The evidence supports the view that liberalization reallocated resources within New Zealand agriculture rather than raising its measured productivity. It gives no support to the opposite claim either: losing assistance worth 35% of output value did not leave the sector behind comparable economies that kept their support in place.

detail.abstract: The curvature of the demand feedback determines the strategic structure of labour-replacing automation. A firm that adopts AI to replace labour keeps the whole cost saving but bears only its share of the fall in demand that follows from lost worker income. When the demand loss is linear, as in the externality studied by Falk and Tsoukalas, automation is a dominant strategy. When demand is convex in automation, the marginal demand cost falls as other firms automate, so automation becomes a strategic complement, and decentralised adoption can lock an industry into an inefficient high-automation equilibrium. I study this as a game among N firms of unequal size in which private benefit, cost and revenue all scale with size. At interior equilibria the aggregate solves one scalar equation in which market structure enters only through the Herfindahl-Hirschman index, and when each firm's own payoff is concave the greatest Nash equilibrium automates at least as much as the joint-profit optimum. Because demand is convex in automation, the game has strategic complements. In the symmetric case there are at most two interior equilibria plus a no-automation corner, and in an explicit parameter window no automation and high automation are both stable symmetric equilibria. Best-response dynamics from the firms' private automation optimum converge monotonically to the greatest equilibrium, which gives every firm its lowest equilibrium payoff; numerical experiments show the same selection under projected gradient play when each firm's own payoff is concave. The payoffs form an exact potential game, and the high-automation outcome is coordination on a local maximum of the potential. Under the same concavity condition, labour displacement is at least as large at the greatest Nash equilibrium as at the joint optimum, and in the multiplicity window the unstable equilibrium is a tipping threshold that rises with market concentration. A Pigouvian tax set at the planner's marginal externality corrects marginal incentives but can leave a jointly worse equilibrium in place. Curvature thus decides the game: linear feedback gives a dominant strategy, convex demand gives complements and multiplicity, and a convex-loss variant (concave demand) gives substitutes and a unique equilibrium.

detail.abstract: Using rich panel micro-data on labor force participation status, we show that India's low female labor force participation reflects not only low entry into employment, but also extremely high exits. Employed women are seven times as likely as men to exit into non-participation, even conditional on demographics, including marriage and education. These exits are largely to home production and are persistent. We document that employment protections are associated with substantially lower exits for women - assigning exit rates of protected women to unprotected women could raise steady-state participation by 21% of the baseline.

detail.abstract: Remote, island, and low-density peripheries face a structural disaster governance dilemma: statutory emergency agencies operate on episodic, post-disaster budgets, making standing village-level monitoring posts fiscally prohibitive. During 7-to-14-day disaster failstates, centralized response hierarchies can experience 48-to-72-hour informational latency as telecommunications collapse. While automated remote sensing exhibits orbital, canopy, and threshold-only blind spots, residents and paraprofessional health workers engaged in routine mobility can function as a Community Early-Warning Network capable of stochastic precursor detection. However, regressive per-capita capitation formulas threaten low-density rural clinics with insolvency and closure, stripping peripheries of ground-level situational awareness. This conceptual working paper formalizes a comparative framework of Opportunistic Fiscal Arbitrage—defined as cross-budget cost sharing rather than riskless profit—across Thailand and Russia. By integrating early-warning and crisis triage protocols into Thailand's Subdistrict Health-Promoting Hospitals (SDHPHs) and Village Health Volunteers (VHVs/OrSorMor) alongside Russia's Feldsher-Midwife Stations (FAPs) and rural assistants, the framework aims to support continuous surveillance without new civil-service DRR payroll lines, funded instead through a pooled Availability Premium. We present a Poisson hazard-adjusted expected-value formulation alongside 2026 stipend parity baselines, outline operational complementarity with Thailand's civil defense volunteers (OrPorPorRor), and examine Tambon Health Funds, Provincial Administrative Organization (PAO) devolution, and Russian concessions/Self-Regulating Organizations (SROs) as candidate legal vehicles. Finally, we specify testable hypotheses—covering a clinical Administrative Firewall and an illustrative 340/25-day AI-assisted versus analog drill ratio for zero-tech packet routing—within a three-paper empirical verification agenda.

detail.abstract: In Australia's Murray-Darling Basin (MDB), short-term (allocation) and long-term (entitlement) water rights are separately traded, centrally reported, and disseminated to the public.  We utilize this setting to demonstrate three primary findings concerning water rights and climate change risk.  First, water rights appear to be a climate change hedge: in periods of diminishing supply, allocation cash flows spike as price increases offset quantity declines. Second, since 2014, entitlement prices in climate-exposed areas have increased by approximately $2,660 per megalitre more than prices in non-climate-exposed areas, over 80% of the 2025 median price of non-exposed entitlements. Allocation prices in the two groups have moved closely together, but they rise more in climate-exposed areas in dry periods. These price differences provide a clear market signal about future scarcity and help define investment opportunities available today to preserve water resources. Finally, estimating the allocation cash-flow to rainfall elasticity and extrapolating with the runoff projections behind the 2014 IPCC assessment, we attribute about 10\% of the price effect to differences in expected cash flow, and the remainder to a lower discount rate. The premium we estimate equates to a 1.7 percentage point lower rate of return for climate hedge or mitigation assets, a critical parameter in climate economics.

detail.abstract: This paper investigates whether U.S. import tariff shocks transmit internationally not only through real trade flows, but as financial shocks. Using structural innovations to the transitory and permanent components of the U.S. tariff rate identified via a Bayesian state-space model, we trace their dynamic transmission to an explicit synthetic Global Financial Conditions Index (GFCI) and a panel of international capital flows across 42 advanced and emerging economies over 1994-2024. We establish four central findings. First, U.S. tariff hikes induce a tightening across several components of global financial conditions: market volatility jumps, the broad U.S. dollar appreciates, and emerging market sovereign risk spreads widen by approximately 100 basis points. While the point estimate for the synthetic GFCI on impact is not statistically distinguishable from zero, it displays significant delayed tightening under permanent shocks and a medium-term rebound under transitory measures. Second, tariff shocks trigger pronounced cross-border capital-flow retrenchments, driven primarily by portfolio debt securities. Under transitory shocks, capital flows rebound within four to six quarters as temporary protectionist measures expire; under permanent shocks, external capital access remains depressed across the two-year policy transmission horizon. Third, crosscountry heterogeneity is stateand persistence-dependent: emerging market economies display substantially greater vulnerability to transitory shocks, whereas permanent protectionist measures produce comparatively larger short-term portfolio retrenchments in advanced economies. Fourth, Two-Way Fixed Effects specifications provide evidence consistent with a balance-sheet vulnerability channel, as capital retrenchments are amplified in economies with elevated U.S. dollar-denominated debt burdens. Trade policy persistence is therefore an important determinant of international financial stability.

detail.abstract: The 2026 war, US naval pressure on Iran's southern routes and its disruption plan (Task force Iron gate) toward land routes have turned Tehran's looking north from a diplomatic preference into a strategic necessity. This essay reads Tehran's recent diplomacy towards Azerbaijan, Armenia, Russia and Central Asia as a two-stage strategy: redundancy, so that no single corridor can strangle the economy, and reach, a central role in Eurasian networks. It argues that positional assets do not produce leverage automatically. Leverage requires interdependence weighted in Iran's favour, which the Aras corridor provides over Baku but TRIPP threatens to erode. Conversion depends on policy coherence, implementation capacity and partners' outside options, with the Rasht-Astara railway as the first test.

title: Optimal Harvest

detail.title: Optimal Harvest

declarations.declarationOfInterest: None

detail.abstract: Optimal f (Vince 1990, 2019) says what fraction of a stake to risk. Nothing in the literature of trading says what fraction to take out. The silence is a consequence and not an oversight: a criterion that maximizes geometric growth can only regard a withdrawal as a wound, and so returns the answer nothing, ever, which no one who has traded for a living believes. We show that the question acquires a definite answer once the account is distinguished from the fortune. The account is the money at the venue; the fortune is all that the trader has. They differ in fact, and not merely in name, wherever there is a hazard that falls upon the account as an account and without regard to the fraction being risked within it: the venue that fails, the custodian that defaults, the loss that lies beyond the largest loss in any spectrum the trader thought to write down. Against such hazards Optimal f is no defense, for they do not act through f. Two results follow. First, the oldest rule of the trading floor, to bank a fixed fraction w of every new-high profit, is the drawdown-optimal policy of Grossman and Zhou (1993) under another name, and equally the active and inactive equity of Vince (1992) with the inactive part carried off the premises. It places beneath the fortune a floor that no run of losses can break, the fortune's worst drawdown being exactly the complement of w, at a price in growth that is linear in w. Second, when the account bears a hazard of rate h, the growth of the fortune is greatest when the account is traded at the Optimal f , undisturbed, and the fraction banked is the hazard divided by the growth rate, w * = h/g * : equivalently, the time the strategy needs to multiply its stake by e, divided by the expected life of the game. Simulation places the optimum at the predicted value. We are explicit that the floor is a restatement of prior work, that a policy which refills the account after losses grows somewhat faster, and that the hazard is a judgment and not an estimate. The orchard is planted by one rule and picked by another, and this paper is about the picking.

detail.abstract: An S-shaped cardinal utility, bounded below and above, represents the fulfilment of an individual's need by a commodity, with increasing marginal utility expressing deprivation. A utility function is created by adding two normal cumulative distribution functions, with subsistence and intensity-of-need parameters, and satiation at infinity. A straightline indifference curve, with slope defined by relative intensity of need, separates concave-to-the-origin indifference curves (dysfunctional poverty) from convex ones. Equations for boundaries between normal inferior and Giffen responses are derived. The labour and consumption diagrams display: involuntary unemployment, disjointed curves, extreme instability, sticky wages and prices, wage-and priceelasticity associated with deprivation, and envelope curves. Engel diagrams reveal that endowments of unearned consumption/income above a significant minimum threshold are essential for a healthy economy based on a healthy society. Labour and consumption are envisaged as complex surfaces in 3-dimensional space with real wages and unearned consumption.

detail.abstract: We examine the impact of the post-2018 legalization of sports betting on the U.S. nonprofit sector. Exploiting the variation in the timing of state betting market launches, we document a significant decline in nonprofit staff payroll following the legalization of sports betting. Employment and employee benefits also decline. NPOs also reduce fundraising expenditure. Cross-sectional analyses suggest that the payroll decline is significant among NPOs highly reliant on public donations but not among hospitals that rely primarily on fees. Furthermore, the estimates for aggregate charitable gaming revenue are positive, while pull-tab revenues decline. Our findings suggest unintended spillover effects of legal sports betting, which are consistent with traditional NPOs reducing labor costs in anticipation of pressure on household giving.

detail.abstract: This study evaluates US hydrogen supply-chain costs and investment competitiveness from 2027 to 2045 without incentives. Commodity-price distributions cover five power markets; learned forecasts are retained where they outperform a drift benchmark. Hierarchical Bayesian models estimate equipment costs, vehicle prices, learning rates and electrolyser deployment. A common cost engine compares six production routes, six storage options and five delivery modes with end-use incumbents, including on-site power and fleet make-or-buy decisions. Median central-plant costs in 2030 are $1.08/kg for gray hydrogen and $6.01/kg for green hydrogen; green hydrogen falls to $5.18/kg by 2045. At 15 MW, on-site hydrogen power costs $306/MWh against $88/MWh for grid electricity. Among the selected 2030 investment cases, positive net present value occurs in at least 80% of model draws for 1,000 forklifts producing hydrogen on site, 250 trucks buying delivered hydrogen and 500 trucks producing on site. These shares are conditional model outputs. Learning-curve inversion estimates deployment-linked expenditure and identifies operating-cost floors. Under the modelled electricity prices, removing electrolyser capital cost is insufficient to achieve gray-hydrogen parity. The results distinguish opportunities governed by equipment learning from those requiring lower energy prices or higher infrastructure utilization.

detail.abstract: Multi-node distribution networks must detect failing nodes quickly, trust the data they act on, and avoid unnecessary intervention. This paper evaluates by simulation a governance architecture adapted from a stylized institutional framework (Vo, 2026): independent supply chain data assurance, a predefined safety fuse, and capacity-limited human review of exceptions. A paired Monte Carlo model of 30 distribution centres over 52 weeks compares it with conventional management and control variants. Under synthetic assumptions, the architecture lowers annual cost by about USD 0.85 million against monthly discretionary management, but only about USD 25,000 (0.4%) against a strong weekly baseline. The advantage reverses when conventional data are timely, when verifying a flag costs more than about USD 570, when independent measurement is noisy or often unavailable, or when review capacity is one case a week; when interventions are weak, no governance design beats doing nothing. Timeliness appears to explain most of the advantage; independence as such was not shown to matter economically. Main contrasts replicate on independent seeds. Inputs are synthetic and single-tier, so the results are a feasibility map, not an empirical estimate.

detail.abstract: This article examines whether Asian economies grew rich because of market liberalization or through sequenced combinations of private incentives, state capacity, structural transformation, and external support. A historical legislative and policy ledger documents 45 events in 18 Asian economies, while the harmonized data comprise 45,407 country-year records drawn from Maddison, Penn World Table, World Development Indicators, institutional indexes, and other uploaded datasets. The principal strategy triangulates legal event timing, long-run income counterfactuals, within-country modern institutional variation, heterogeneity interactions, and falsification tests rather than imposing one time-invariant definition of economic freedom. The analysis combines capital-labor-productivity growth accounting, convergence regressions and log-t screening, endogenous multiple-break and unit-root diagnostics, historical country-and time-weighted counterfactuals, staggered-cohort comparisons with not-yet-treated Asian cases, actual applied-tariff measurements, positive and negative index movements, commodity-price interactions, aid-flow shocks, crisis interactions, and outlier-robust tariff placebo tests. Penn World Table yields 825 complete annual national-accounting decompositions; WDI provides 3,806 tariff-rate and 10,203 official-development-assistance observations in the harmonized panel. Twelve policy episodes admit weighted counterfactual comparisons, while additional country-held-out orthogonal machine-learning estimates and threshold diagnostics expose learner sensitivity and poor overlap. The tariff-growth association for Asia is particularly fragile: its initially negative and significant coefficient changes sign and loses significance when extreme annual tariff changes or Nepal are excluded, and a negative-control regression associates tariff movements with earlier growth. The Asian cross-sectional convergence slope changes sign between 1960-1990 and 1990-2020, while full-sample transition-convergence tests reject homogeneity. Strong growth around reform episodes therefore cannot be uniquely attributed to market opening. Documented pretrends, policy bundling, endogenous dates, donor contamination and measurement problems prevent a single reliable causal estimate of "free markets." The evidence is consistent with heterogeneous, sequenced market-state complementarities but does not identify their separate causal contributions.

detail.abstract: Model validation consists of multiple tests against reported VaR and ES values: failure-ratio and independence tests (Kupiec, Christoffersen's independence), a conditional-coverage test, and an exception count (Basel). A model is validated only if all of them are passed. This paper asks the reverse question: taking as fixed the observed outcomes of a model over a historical period, what is the lowest VaR and, for a given ES-to-VaR relationship, the lowest ES it can forecast while every test still passes? We term this series the Maximum Undetectable Lie, expressed as a basis-point understatement, a dollar understatement for a specified notional, or the additional exceptions allowed per year. For an AAPL 99 per cent VaR over the latest 250 days, one greedy approach hides 249 basis points, about $24.9 million on a $1 billion notional, and every regulatory gate stays green. The mixed-integer program certifies the greatest underestimate: it hides 29 to 33 per cent more than the corresponding greedy construction. Adding the anytime-valid e-process ES test of Wang, Wang and Ziegel invalidates the naive attacker outright, but removes only about 1 per cent of the lie from an e-aware attacker; the surviving understatement is context-dependent, not universal.

detail.abstract:
We study two-sided assortment revenue maximization when supplier
display revenue functions are normalized, monotone, and submodular.
Customers initiate interactions, and suppliers respond after all
customer choices have been observed. Cardinality constraints may
apply to either or both sides. Given an \(\alpha\)-approximate oracle
for weighted customer assortment optimization, we develop a
randomized polynomial-time policy with approximation guarantee
\((1-2/e^2)(1-e^{-\alpha})-\varepsilon\) against the optimal
customer-initiated adaptive policy. The guarantee improves to
\(1-e^{-\alpha}-\varepsilon\) when every supplier display limit
is one or nonbinding.

Our approach combines a joint marginal relaxation, an
\(\alpha\)-preserving reduction to customer assortment optimization,
and a non-oblivious potential that compares the multilinear
objective directly with a correlated upper bound on the adaptive
optimum. We construct feasible supplier displays using revenue
evaluations and contention resolution, without requiring an exact
oracle for the constrained pool value. In the common unit-revenue
setting with monotone submodular demand on both sides, our results
improve the guarantees of \citet{housni2026two} against the same
adaptive benchmark. With exact customer oracles, we improve their
\(1/2\) guarantee to \(1-1/e-\varepsilon\) in the unconstrained and
initiating-side regimes, and their \((1-1/e)^3-\varepsilon\)
guarantee to \((1-2/e^2)(1-1/e)-\varepsilon\) in the responding-side
and two-way regimes. For approximate customer oracles, we extend
their LP-policy analysis to obtain
\(\alpha(1-1/e)^3-\varepsilon\) and show that our uniform guarantee
\((1-2/e^2)(1-e^{-\alpha})-\varepsilon\) improves on this bound
for every \(\alpha\in(0,1]\).

detail.abstract: New ventures in Central Europe grow up inside institutional environments that are neither fully mature nor fully void. Formal rules have converged on European Union standards, yet capital markets remain thin, informal ties remain consequential, and successful technology ventures frequently exit to foreign exchanges. At the same time, artificial intelligence and related digital technologies are altering what a new venture is, who acts on its behalf, and how investors evaluate it. This conceptual paper integrates institutional theory, signaling and legitimacy perspectives on initial public offerings, and research on technological disruption to explain how these forces jointly shape new venture performance in the region. We develop seven propositions. We argue that the IPO operates as a legitimacy substitute whose value rises where market-supporting intermediaries are weak, that positive media sentiment exhibits a too-muchof-a-good-thing effect that is sharper in thin markets, and that founder drive pays off most when paired with political skill in particularistic settings. We further propose that category-breaking ventures face an initial valuation discount but superior long-run performance, that artificial intelligence acting as an entrepreneurial actor weakens the dependence of performance on local institutions, and that organizational scope and supranational harmonization condition these relationships. We conclude with a research agenda and implications for founders, investors, exchanges, and policymakers.

title: The Firm as a Bargain over Risk

detail.abstract: Why do capable, well-informed people accept direction by others inside firms, and why do so many later leave to found firms of their own? Coase's answer rests on the costs of using the price mechanism, which later work has largely interpreted as costs of information, contracting and enforcement. This paper argues that such costs do not explain who directs whom, why the directed accept direction, or why they later exit. I propose that the employment relation is better understood as a bargain over risk: employees obtain security by ceding authority, and residual claimants obtain authority because they bear the downside of the decisions they direct. The argument reformulates Knight's theory of the firm and the Kihlstrom-Laffont model, treating the capacity to bear risk as a resource accumulated during employment, and links them to Taleb's principle of skin in the game. From an evolutionary perspective, I argue that the bargain rests on older arrangements: in primates, rank combines privileges, costs and services to followers; in human foragers, deference is conditional and sanctioned by coalitions; food sharing insured against variance; and heritable variation in risk tolerance, maintained by selection, supports a natural division of risk-bearing. The paper derives testable implications concerning exit and founding, insurance within firms, and the fate of authority detached from exposure, and discusses objections including holdup and managers who command without bearing risk.

detail.abstract: Do investors forgive bad corporate news when the president is popular? Using 521,585 earnings announcements by 15,284 U.S. firms from 1993 to 2025 and monthly Gallup approval, I find that when approval is one standard deviation above the president's own term average, the announcement penalty for negative earnings surprises is 20 percent smaller, and the stocks do not give back the difference over the next sixty trading days. The response to positive surprises is unchanged. A simple valuation model links this asymmetry to the persistence of bad news, and negative surprises indeed carry over about 23 percent less to the next quarter when approval is high. The effect survives controls for consumer sentiment, volatility, recessions, and policy uncertainty, and the removal of any single president. The honeymoon of a new presidency, treated as a discrete episode, shows no reliable effect.

detail.abstract: In securities litigation, experts frequently use the returns of other firms within the defendant's industry as a benchmark. But some corrective disclosures impact the prices of these peer firms. When a defendant's corrective disclosure reveals that other firms in the industry had inflated share prices due to a similar material misstatement, plaintiff classes may be defined too narrowly. Conversely, when the defendant's corrective-disclosure transfers economic rents to peer firms, industry adjustments may cause experts to overestimate damages. Using a dataset of 1,713 securities class actions and 4,002 corrective-disclosures spanning 2015-2026, this paper documents that it is common for peers to have abnormal returns on corrective-disclosure dates. Disclosure spillovers have increased over time, a trend that coincides with a well-documented increase in return synchronicity likely driven by growth of index-investing and ETFs and an increased reliance on common technologies like AI.

detail.abstract: Problem Definition: AI-enabled operational systems increasingly embed algorithmic recommendations in recurring workflows where human decision makers can modify them before an operational decision is finalized. Such interventions may contain information that could improve subsequent algorithmic recommendations. However, even across repeated interactions, the resulting records may not reveal whether such information is transferable. An intervention may be useful for the current decision without providing evidence reliable enough for persistent learning. Methodology/Results: We propose Use-Learn Evidence Gating (ULEG), an evidence-governance architecture with separate rules for current use and persistent learning. The current-use rule depends on ex-ante distinctiveness and inherited long-term credibility; the learning rule applies a stricter standard combining ex-ante distinctiveness with ex-post outcome support. We instantiate this architecture in demand forecasting and evaluate it through controlled simulations and a real-data-grounded semi-synthetic analysis using M5 demand paths and observed selling prices. ULEG's relative advantage is clearest when algorithmic forecasts remain systematically misaligned with demand, as when the algorithm does not fully adjust to changing conditions, and human interventions vary in informativeness. ULEG also provides a framework for optimizing current use and persistent learning separately against an operating objective. In the inventory case, this optimization reduces cost compared to the default ULEG solution and achieves lower average order amplification relative to directly optimizing the use weight and learning intensity. Managerial Implications: ULEG allows managers to set separate evidence requirements for using human adjustments in current decisions and admitting the resulting evidence into persistent learning. An adjustment can therefore influence today's decision without automatically becoming part of tomorrow's algorithmic baseline. These controls help managers benefit from timely human information while limiting the persistence of unreliable adjustments and retaining the ability to correct systematic baseline errors.

detail.abstract: In 2019 Brazil abolished daylight saving time, moving an hour of summer light from evening to morning for 131 million people. We compare road deaths in the clock hour that turned dark in each municipality and day with the same hour in states that kept standard time. These deaths rose 34 percent, and pedestrians account for 43 percent of the increase. The effect follows the local sun, not the clock, and the brighter mornings showed no detectable decline in deaths. If hours whose light did not change were unaffected, abolition added 62 crash-scene deaths each summer, mid-November to mid-February.

detail.abstract: We apply Bayesian persuasion-based information design to craft influencer strategy in a market with independent third-party review platforms (TPRPs). These reputation-conscious entities engage in "half-truths"-they sometimes make Type II errors by reviewing wellmatched products as bad. In contrast, an influencer posts biased reviews that reflect their trade-off between earning commissions and improving consumer welfare. We endogenize firm choices related to influencer engagement, contracts, and product pricing. We find that the optimal influencer strategy is sensitive to the TPRP's error rate: The firm optimally uses an influencer when the TPRP's Type II error is low to moderate. Surprisingly, we find that the firm should use an influencer who maximizes consumer welfare when the TPRP's Type II error is low. Now the influencer posts "helpful lies" by framing a bad match as a good one. These lies address the under-adoption of well-matched products and increase consumer welfare. In contrast, when the TPRP's Type II error is moderate, the firm chooses a salesoriented influencer and motivates them through sales commissions. Counterintuitively, when the TPRP's Type II error is high, the firm skips influencers all together. Our findings inform the design of influencer strategy in the presence of TPRPs.

detail.abstract: Taking the juxtaposition of Sam's Club and Aldi in Shanghai as a case, this paper asks how two almost opposite retail models can take root and earn a profit in the same city. Existing explanations appeal to purchasing power, to format positioning, or to the capabilities of foreign firms. This paper proposes a three-part structure of time, space and symbol. Sam's Club sells "two hours of the weekend"; Aldi sells "fifteen minutes after work." The first rests on the car-borne ring beyond the outer ring road, the second on the walkable ring inside it. The first manufactures institutional trust-"I chose the right system"through a membership card; the second manufactures price transparency-"I was not taken in"through the price tag. The three structures reinforce one another and jointly lower the consumer's cost of choosing. Shanghai can hold both kinds of time not because it is richer but because four conditions hold at once: a thick and continuous middle in the income distribution, a sharply layered urban space, a supply chain in the Yangtze River Delta close at hand, and small, ageing households that arrived earlier than elsewhere. The paper further argues that the two firms are not each other's principal rival. Their common opponent is a retail environment of low price, low quality and low trust, and their boundary lies not in format but in whether a city still contains enough people willing to pay for certainty.

detail.abstract: Employee engagement remains a central construct in human resource management research and practice, yet persistent ambiguity surrounding its conceptualization continues to limit theoretical integration and practical application. This paper offers a contemporary conceptual synthesis of employee engagement by integrating foundational psychological theory with organizational and human resource management perspectives. Drawing on classical engagement frameworks, including Kahn's psychological conditions of engagement and the Job Demands-Resources model, the paper develops an integrative conceptual framework that positions engagement as an emergent psychological state shaped by organizational structures, leadership practices, and resource systems. The framework highlights how engagement arises from the interaction between individual psychological conditions and organizational enablers, producing multi-level outcomes for employees, teams, and organizations. By situating engagement within evolving work contexts, including flexible and hybrid arrangements, this paper clarifies construct boundaries, reconciles competing perspectives, and advances a systems-oriented understanding of engagement. The paper concludes by outlining implications for human resource management theory and practice and proposing directions for future research aimed at sustaining engagement in contemporary organizations.

detail.abstract: Using Pop Mart's 2025 annual report, its 2026 interim report and its third-quarter announcement as a sample, this report asks whether a traffic-driven IP platform can convert short-lived heat into durable brand equity. It proposes a distinction between container IP and script IP. A container IP carries the consumer's self-projection through silhouette and blank space: it expands fast and lives short. A script IP sustains cross-generational identification through narrative and character relations: it expands slowly and lasts. Pop Mart's growth rests on container IP, and its financial structure therefore shows a distinctive combination — high gross margin, high operating expense, high inventory and weak reversion. The report builds four observable thresholds for the passage from traffic to brand — licensing revenue share, repurchase rate, gross margin and resale premium — and argues that the binding constraints lie not in demand but in property rights (most IP is licensed rather than owned outright) and in price discipline (scarcity can be switched on and off, but not tuned). The conclusion is that the cooling of heat is only a gear change: whether it settles into a brand depends on whether the company will trade two or three quarters of ugly numbers for stable pricing and stable repurchase.

detail.abstract: Traditional municipal solid waste management systems suffer from severe behavioral friction, relying on non-incentivized civic altruism that fails to offset the cognitive and physical costs of household sorting. This paper introduces the Theory of Cross-Incentives (Teoría de Incentivos Cruzados®) and presents an empirical, cloud-based software architecture designed to transform passive domestic waste into immediate, bankable consumption assets. Operating via asynchronous messaging APIs and singleuse dynamic cryptographic tokens (OTP/TTL), the system eliminates localized hardware dependencies while ensuring regulatory immunity from traditional fintech saving instruments. Furthermore, to guarantee long-term server and financial sustainability, the architecture implements an automated double-entry accounting algorithm (Cron Job) that extinguishes inactive digital balances at day 91, preserving latent user UUIDs while redirecting unredeemed accounting value toward tax-deductible non-profit donations. Validated across five years of continuous commercial operations in Mexico (2011-2016) and updated through 2026 under patent-pending frameworks (USPTO No. 64/194,061), the model empirically diverted over 780 metric tons of clean post-consumer materials from landfills, preventing 156,000 liters of toxic leachate contamination and saving over 10.8 million liters of industrial water. These findings provide a replicable econometric baseline for scaling decentralized circular ecosystems and mitigating localized methane (CH4) emissions across urban settlements.

detail.abstract: An airline that advertises a Paris-aligned target may have to justify the impression it gives passengers long before the target falls due. Whether anyone can compel the airline to cut its emissions raises a different legal question. This article examines how far domestic law can hold firms to the climate commitments on which international cooperation increasingly draws. I compare how courts, regulators and voluntary initiatives in the European Union, the United Kingdom, Australia, Singapore and the United States review issuer disclosures, descriptions of financial products, consumer advertising and membership commitments. Across these settings, accountability depends on substantiation, the prohibited defect, fault, the audience protected, access to proceedings and the relief available. Whereas the Amsterdam District Court declared KLM's advertisements misleading and the Federal Court of Australia ordered fund providers to publicise adverse findings about their investment screens, a shareholder seeking to alter Shell's climate strategy failed even to obtain permission to litigate on the company's behalf. I describe this institutional divergence as selective legalisation. Domestic law gives particular consequences to what a firm tells investors or consumers, while the underlying pledge may remain voluntary. European disputes over prior verification and Singapore's phased reporting rules expose a further choice about who pays to test such claims. Where publicity is optional, firms may respond by saying less, even when their environmental practices continue.

In this sample, women report expected earnings 28.4 percent lower than men after certification. The gap becomes much smaller after accounting for vocational field, but the within-field estimates are too imprecise to determine the sign or magnitude of the remaining difference. Perceived average earnings in related work display a similar raw-versus-within-field pattern. Possible mechanisms include differences in information and occupational preferences, as well as gendered constraints related to care responsibilities, schedules, and anticipated work flexibility.

detail.abstract: This essay reports what three readers saw in the same wall. The Rorschach Zeitgeist LLM Test presents sixteen cell-phone photographs of knockdown and orange-peel drywall texture and asks two large language models, Claude (Anthropic) and GPT (OpenAI), each to outline and number the figures it finds, to code each one as a Rorschach response is coded, to read each against nine historical epochs, and to answer the author's questions about the workers who made the walls. Each system returned 160 figures, ten per photograph, and their findings are set side by side here, photograph by photograph. The two registers agree where the protocol or the photographs constrain them: both make pre-history the most frequent epoch (46 and 44 figures), their epoch distributions overlap on 87% of assignments, and both find the same repeated views of one wall. They differ in what they saw and in how far they would go. Claude saw movement where GPT saw objects (62 kinetic figures against 19), and Claude answered the questions about the makers where GPT held that the photographs cannot answer them. In a third stage the fixed count of ten was removed. The author and both systems each read one photograph under a single rule, to stop when no further figure is apparent without being forced. The author reported 24 figures, Claude 43, and GPT 9, and 5 on a second pass. The author's figures are larger and assembled from several patches of the wall; all but one are living things; and ten of them were marked by neither system. Three regions were marked by all three readers and received three different names each time. The essay sets the historical lens of Freud and Jung beside the lens of current cognitive science, holds that neither is wholly correct, and keeps the author's null reading open: the marks may be random, and the figures belong to the finder.

detail.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is used by the vast majority of companies, but only a small share translates its adoption into measurable business value. This paper argues that the gap stems less from the technology than from the absence of a strategy that consistently derives both the point of deployment and the precise task of AI from business goals, across the entire workflow up to its outcome. Individual use cases may be well chosen; without this end-toend derivation, however, they remain local optimizations. Since AI is hard to control while firms depend on reliability, such a strategy must reconcile both. Building on a definition of strategy as an adaptive program, the paper conceives AI functionally as a supplier of information at decision points and locates its value where information bottlenecks constrain critical outcomes on the path to business goals. A review of six widely used or recent approaches shows that they support the identification of AI opportunities but provide no standardized procedure for locating the leverage points at which AI should apply. The paper deductively derives the Enterprise AI Strategy Framework, consisting of three guiding principles and eight building blocks connected by two feedback loops. Its core is the Critical Outcome Path (CROP), a standardized backward derivation from the critical outcome via the decision and its information requirements to the point of AI deployment. Built around CROP, the framework transfers prior workflow-level research to the level of the firm and gives managers a repeatable method for deciding where, why and how to use AI. As a conceptual contribution, it has not yet been empirically validated.

detail.abstract: Reports of AI visibility often present a citation rate as a trend line. This paper asks how much of a reported movement can come from the counting specification and repetition noise rather than changed answers. It recounts saved runs from one project: 48 informational prompts, three repetitions each, collected twice on 1 November 2026 through a ChatGPT scraper and a Gemini scraper under identical settings. Twenty domain and scraper pairs, the ten most cited domains per scraper in the first sweep, are scored under ten counting rules, and moves are judged against relabeling nulls. For one domain, the repeat sweep gave 27 of 144 runs (18.75%) over all prompts and 23 of 45 runs (51.11%) over the prompts that had cited it in the first sweep. These are run-presence rates on different prompt populations. A share of 27 of 647 citation slots (4.17%) uses a different unit and is not a comparable rate. Across the 20 pairs the selected-prompt rate was a median 4.0 times the default rate (range 2.1 to 12.0). Under the specified selection-only null, 18 of 20 observed selected-prompt rates fell within the central 95% simulation range; this is a compatibility result under an exchangeability assumption, not evidence that selection caused the difference. The direction of the change between the two sweeps depended on the counting rule for 10 of 20 pairs. The largest of ten selected moves reached 7 runs in 52% to 63% of relabelings, against 0% to 26% for a single domain chosen in advance. Between 49% and 68% of the variance in a domain's citation outcome (median over domains) lay between repetitions within a sweep, and 0% to 4% lay between sweeps. The records support a methods demonstration, not a population estimate: one date, one repeat, two scrapers and one project's prompts. The paper closes with a reporting checklist derived from these results.

detail.abstract:
US Congress mandated more accurate broadband mapping through the Broadband DATA Act of 2020. In 2022, the Federal Communication Commission (FCC) launched the Broadband Data Collection (BDC) program, composed of the Fabric Challenge, Fixed Availability Challenge, and Mobile Availability Challenge. Each of these challenges inform how Broadband Equity, Access, and Deployment (BEAD) funding is allocated to specific states regions to ensure that areas without a minimum level of broadband service are prioritized. Importantly, these challenge processes enable “consumers, Tribes, governments, providers, and [other citizens] to continually improve and refine the accuracy of the broadband availability data.” 

While a number of studies have examined results from the Fabric Challenge and Fixed Availability Challenge, there has been a lack of attention on the Mobile Availability Challenge  (MAC) results, despite growing trend of smartphone dependence among different demographic groups. Indeed, as of February 2026, there have only been 378 cognizable MAC challenges between September 2023 and April 2026. In this paper we use Ookla Mobile Performance data to reveal how current MAC data does not necessarily reflect places where coverage needs to be challenged. This highlights an important gap between attempted participation/non-participation and successful challenges that require new approaches.

To examine these approaches, we investigate the feasibility of leveraging federal fleet vehicles to opportunistically collect data as part of the MAC process. We show that this approach could increase measurement of locations that are currently reported as having full mobile broadband coverage by 91.7%. We also show that this approach captures 48% of rural MAC hexagons and 42.1% of Ookla's slow tiles (<35 Mbps) in rural areas, indicating that it is likely to cover existing areas of interest. At the end of this paper, we discuss how broadband regulators and advocates can support greater participation in the MAC.

detail.abstract: Firms increasingly claim artificial intelligence (AI) capability, yet investors and regulators have few means of verifying such claims. This gap creates room for AI washing and gives firms a reason to ask whether vague AI talk carries consequences when another firm faces enforcement. We frame AI capability disclosure as a corporate governance problem and combine disclosure measurement with a Fama-French three-factor event study. Drawing on cheap talk theory, we use a transparent index of strategic ambiguity to distinguish how extensively firms discuss AI from how precisely they describe their capabilities in 96,733 SEC filings by S&P 1500 firms from 2022 to 2026. When two SEC cases challenged AI claims, firms outside the proceedings that had discussed AI more extensively earned lower five-day abnormal returns than peers that had said less. Around three announcements of prospective AI rules, the relationship was slightly positive. The extent of prior AI discussion distinguished firms' market exposure across policy settings, while evidence of invention helped explain how markets interpreted ambiguous disclosures. In a separate analysis of civil enforcement, the negative relationship between disclosure ambiguity and returns weakened as firms' AI patent activity increased. We explain these findings through signaling theory, which suggests that enforcement draws attention to what firms have claimed and that patents give investors an observable basis for assessing those claims. We offer regulators, boards, and investors a practical way to distinguish AI capability from AI rhetoric by matching each claim to evidence of what the firm has invented or put into use.

detail.abstract: AI agents are beginning to search, compare and pay on behalf of consumers. Between late 2024 and late 2026, model developers, payment networks, payment service providers and commerce platforms released a dense set of open protocols for this purpose, including the Agentic Commerce Protocol, the Agent Payments Protocol, the Universal Commerce Protocol, Visa's Trusted Agent Protocol, Mastercard Agent Pay and the x402 standard. Early deployments have been uneven, and the academic literature remains fragmented across computer science, economics, law and marketing. This paper offers a conceptual synthesis of what we call frontier agentic commerce: purchasing in which an AI agent holds delegated decision rights and, increasingly, delegated spending authority. We make four contributions. First, we propose a five level autonomy ladder (L0 to L4) that separates human present from human not present commerce and links each level to the trust infrastructure it requires. Second, we review the emerging protocol landscape and organise it into a seven layer agentic commerce stack running from intent and mandate to dispute and recourse. Third, we analyse the consequences for marketing and search, arguing that persuasion shifts from human attention to model inference, which turns search engine optimisation into what we call agent facing optimisation and makes structured product data, verifiable trust signals and earned media the new determinants of visibility. Fourth, we map security, competition and consumer protection risks onto the stack and derive twelve research propositions. The framework is intended to give marketing scholars, managers and policymakers a shared vocabulary for a market in which the customer is increasingly a machine acting for a person.

detail.abstract: AI is shifting the balance of power in consumer transactions toward sellers. Algorithmic pricing tools set prices in real time using competitor prices, demand and individual consumer profiles, and seller-side AI agents are now built into major shopping platforms. Consumers face these systems alone. This paper examines how pricing algorithms and seller agents can learn to keep prices high without any agreement between sellers, and why existing competition, product liability and privacy law struggles to assign responsibility for the resulting harm. It reviews recent enforcement and policy developments in the United States, Canada and Europe, and considers legal options including liability for those who design and deploy pricing agents, regulatory sandbox testing, and treating software as a product. Because legal change will be slow, the paper proposes a market response: a personal buyer agent trained on the individual’s own data, secured by a voluntary decentralized digital ID, that acts for the consumer against seller agents. It closes with the risks of such agents and the safeguards they need, including audit logs, spending limits and human confirmation for transactions that are hard to reverse.

detail.abstract:
An operational record can establish that a human approved an AI-supported decision without settling whether oversight was meaningful or a remedy effective. This conceptual contribution applies a previously proposed evidence-governed Compliance Assessment Framework to selected provisions of UN Human Rights Council Resolution 63/15, adopted in October 2026. It develops an inspectable mapping informed by paragraphs 8, 9, 10 and 13, comprising 22 author-defined assessment elements that retain source addressees, operative force and open qualifiers. It introduces a method-relative evidenceability classification distinguishing directly assessable operational predicates (E1), partially assessable mixed predicates (E2) and judgment-dependent conclusions (E3), with separate atomic subclaims and sourceto-target traceability. Five deliberately synthetic recruitment cases illustrate bounded assessment outcomes without asserting real-world reliability, normative fidelity or human-rights compliance. The paper also discusses an optional enterprise governance pathway, including rights-holder-sensitive impact assessment, human oversight by design and effect verification. Grounded in the final English resolution text, the proposed mapping uses a computer-science and information-security perspective to distinguish source conditions from author-proposed operational predicates and evidence requirements while preserving unresolved legal and human-rights qualifiers. It neither establishes compliance, remedy effectiveness, nor a validated control standard, and it is not a checklist of directly enforceable obligations. Its interpretive adequacy and coverage, classification reliability, assessor independence and practical usefulness remain subjects for independent normative and empirical evaluation, as outlined in the Future Work section.

detail.abstract: Embedding models serve as the foundational layer for modern information retrieval systems, determining how effectively AI systems understand and retrieve relevant information. This paper presents a comprehensive benchmarking study evaluating embedding model optimization techniques using the BEIR (Benchmarking IR) benchmark suite. We fine-tune the E5-base-v2 model using Multiple Negatives Ranking Loss on multiple BEIR datasets and evaluate performance across diverse domains including medical information retrieval, scientific document retrieval, and general semantic similarity tasks. Our optimization approach achieves significant improvements, with up to 51% improvement on Recall@100 for medical information retrieval (NFE Corpus), 20% improvement on scientific document retrieval (SciDocs), while maintaining stable performance on general domain tasks. We further investigate domain-specific finetuning strategies, demonstrating that specialized models often outperform general-purpose multi-dataset models for specific use cases. Our results demonstrate the effectiveness of strategic finetuning techniques and provide insights into the trade-offs between multi-dataset and domain-specific optimization approaches for production information retrieval systems.
